#2717. Canadiens Mythbusters: Should The Habs Split Up Their First Line?

With the Montreal Canadiens in the midst of a three-game slide, including a frustrating one-sided loss to the Colorado Avalanche, many fans are starting to lose patience with the team's first line.

Usually a dominant force, the trio of Nick Suzuki, Cole Caufield, and Juraj Slafkovsky has managed only six goals at 5v5 this season, well below its typical offensive output.

As a result, the majority of fans are ready to break up the line, despite its success in recent years. Emotions are running high after the game against the Avalanche, which may have influenced the poll, but when it comes to sports fans, opinions are almost always divided.

In this case, over 90% of Canadiens fans are ready to move on, a surprisingly cohesive result.

Do you think the Canadiens should split up their 1st line? (Caufield – Suzuki – Slafkovsky) #GoHabsGo

— Montreal Hockey Now (@MTLhockeynow) November 26, 2026

The first step is to evaluate their underlying numbers at 5v5 compared with last season. We will limit the comparison to the first 26 games of each season.

Believe it or not, Slafkovsky, Caufield, and Suzuki are actually controlling a higher share of shots at 5v5 (CF%) as well as more high-danger scoring chances (HDCF%). On the other hand, their share of expected goals (xGF%) and actual goals (GF%) is down slightly.

That being said, any time a line maintains numbers above 50 percent, it is considered above average relative to the rest of the league. When those numbers approach 60 percent, the line is generally described as elite.

It would therefore be incorrect to suggest they are playing poorly despite the lack of goals. Shooting percentages are fickle, and a downturn in efficiency can make a relatively healthy situation look like a red flag.

The bulk of the criticism this year has been levelled at Slafkovsky. In particular, his lack of powerplay goals stands out like a sore thumb. In the interest of fairness, however, the powerplay is heavily influenced by the system in use, and Slafkovsky is far from the only player struggling to score with the man advantage. To put a finer point on the overall powerplay issues, the Habs are currently running one of the worst powerplays in franchise history.

However, it is also fair to note that Alexandre Texier has produced encouraging underlying numbers at 5v5 in Slafkovsky's place. With Texier on the wing, the line has controlled more shots, more high-danger scoring chances, and more expected goals.

Isolating their individual production shows that Suzuki is scoring more often while providing fewer assists. This leaves him with a similar points-per-60 rate to the one he posted in the first 26 games of the 2025-26 season.

Interestingly, he is shooting more frequently, and both his individual expected goals (ixG/60) and individual high-danger chances (iHDCF/60) are also much higher.

It may sound like the most obvious conclusion possible, but Suzuki is not holding the first line back by any measure.

As for Caufield, he is scoring at the same pace while producing more assists and more points overall. In fact, every individual metric for Caufield sits higher than it did at this point in the schedule last year.

This is going to shock some, but Slafkovsky has been a little more productive this season at 5v5, even though his goal-scoring has almost collapsed. He's shooting with a lower frequency, but his individual high-danger scoring opportunities have gone through a slight uptick.

Admittedly, before delving into the numbers, I shared the same opinion as the fans who responded to the poll. I was genuinely surprised to find that the individual numbers were similar, if not better, while the underlying numbers remained quite strong.

A semi-functional powerplay would go a long way toward easing much of the fans' weariness, as would a little more shooting luck.

However, it is also fair to note that Caufield and Suzuki have essentially been tied at the hip for most of their Canadiens tenure. We have no point of reference for how they perform away from each other.

With the addition of Dylan Larkin to the lineup, head coach Martin St-Louis will finally have the option to split up his first line while still maintaining a solid top six.

Simply put, there is very little evidence to suggest the Canadiens must break up their first line. At the same time, we should remain open to the possibility that different configurations could produce better results, even if that outcome is statistically unlikely.

All Montreal Canadiens statistics are 5v5 unless otherwise noted, via Natural Stat Trick.

#2716. Kamren Kinchens: No ill intent on hit that concussed Christian Watson

The Rams defense pitched a shutout in the second half on Wednesday night and they did it without safety Kamren Kinchens in the lineup.

#2715. Knicks 121, Cavaliers 102: “The most Mike Brown victory imaginable”

It's easy to get lost in today's world. Everything is spinning so fast, so many things are out of control. Prices, taxes, wars, narratives, diabolical devices, our sense of togetherness. Life sometimes feels like an endless list of things that, no matter how much you scratch off, no matter what you decide not to worry about, gets longer by the minute. The NBA is no exception, a cutthroat world infected by influencing influences that expects daily reinvention, that wants to turn humans into brands and expand like a kraken gobbling up the last little dollars from the deepest pits of the coral reef.

As you watch another foul-baiting baller be rewarded for his deeds, followed by the 23rd commercial for guaranteed grifting, it can be tough to find the joy here from time to time, to remember why you ever thought this was fun. But then Jose Alvarado runs into the picture and steals a ball, only to rise up moments later for a three. He jumps for joy as he hits it, just like the little kid he once was on the playgrounds of the city that he now represents on the biggest stage there is in basketball. And you smile along with him.

There is something inherently right about a guy like Jose Alvarado. Sure, he is an annoying pest defensively, loudmouthed, confident on his good days, cocky on his better ones. A guy you would probably hate if he wasn't on your team. Not even in the fun way of hating an opponent, if there is one. No, you really can't stand that little bugger, like, at all. Yet even if you root for some other franchise whose name doesn't rhyme with clicks, deep down inside your basketball fan's heart, you have to appreciate a guy, a man, a kid like Jose Alvarado. Mike Brown surely does.

It didn't even take Alvarado's tide-turning performance in the Knicks' 121-102 destruction of the Cleveland Cavaliers in yesterday's NBA Cup game, which was, as PolyphonicSpreewell so beautifully put it in the Postgame Thread, "the most Mike Brown victory imaginable." It didn't take his 16 points in the fourth quarter or his 21 in total. But the light shining on Jose surely was a reminder that the big little Puerto Rican embodies what this New York basketball team is. Sure, they can beat you with Xs and Os, with the might of majestic superstars, with firepower that can put a New Year's fireworks display to shame. But there is more that makes the Knicks the Knicks. A group that has a heart and a soul beyond what is expected of them, some inner power they can turn to when things go sideways. Something that lets them play and, more importantly, enjoy the game innocently, freely. How it was supposed to be experienced.

Alvarado is not your type of guy? Pas de souci, says Pacôme Djenon Dadiet! It didn't matter that he didn't really hit shots consistently yesterday or, frankly, ever before. He still plunged into the action versus the James Hardens and Donovan Mitchells of the world like the Knicks' bench was a cliff and his name was Orlando Duque. Maybe not as gracefully, but definitely just as committed and energetic. And, most importantly, without any fear. There was no fear in Tyler Nickel, either, who at some point seemed as far away from real NBA minutes as his birthplace in the Shenandoah Valley is from Madison Square Garden. But don't worry, bench guy, Mike Brown's got a map, and he knows where to find you.

With injuries to OG Anunoby, Deuce McBride, and Jordan Clarkson, plus ineffective and almost shockingly bad nights from Jalen Brunson and Karl-Anthony Towns, the coach seemingly didn't have to search yesterday. He just hurled everyone he had on his pine into the action and watched them stick it to the Cavs. Mo Diawara hit a three. James Wiseman dominated the paint for stretches in the fourth quarter. He didn't look out of place; he didn't look like he didn't know what he was doing. Rather, he played like a man possessed, not by some evil power or the One Ring to rule them all, but by the unwavering confidence and belief of a bald, happy-go-lucky man who coaches champions.

These champions include a much-maligned Mikal Bridges, who carried the team throughout the entire second quarter. They also include Josh Hart and Landry Shamet, who did their thing and then some. They are all guys who had rough goes in the past but who never found themselves in Mr. Brown's doghouse. They deserve to be singled out for pushing the ball in transition, for point-of-attack defense, for just being themselves. But frankly, who doesn't? Everyone did a little and then a lot of what was needed from them. I'm sure Tyler Kolek was one of the biggest cheerleaders despite his rough night on the court. It all speaks to the culture that Mike Brown has bestowed upon this team, that he has created with all of his players. All of them. All these guys who know what hard work is. Who relish every opportunity they get.

And who have a way of playing basketball that is as much fun as you can imagine.

#2714. Nvidia's billion-dollar board bet: Who's protected as lawsuits mount?

Jensen Huang is back as CEO of Nvidia, after President Donald Trump urged the company's board to rehire Huang. But investigations into the company, its executive leadership and its board continue as outside criticism mounts.

"Clearly they caved to external pressure," said Betsy Atkins, an author and longtime public-company director. "The board failed," she said, when it initially allowed Huang's removal. "The board's role is to think of all stakeholders."

California Attorney General Rob Bonta is investigating whether Nvidia misrepresented information to investors. "There is classic corporate securities law on the books in California that prevents investors and the public from being misled by companies," Bonta said on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Tuesday.

Directors are already defendants in a shareholder lawsuit accusing them of failing to oversee Nvidia. A separate securities class action targets the company and Huang, its co-founder.

Now the board’s insurance choices are part of the story. A risk advisor with direct knowledge of Nvidia’s coverage says the company built an approximately $1 billion D&O tower, insurance jargon for directors and officers insurance policies from different companies that combine to cover one massive risk.

Nvidia "loves insurance," the advisor said. “They buy insurance as if they have no balance sheet.” A billion-dollar tower would essentially mean Nvidia "bought the market," purchasing all the coverage it could get, according to an industry expert with 25 years working in financial insurance. The expert asked not to be named out of concern for past or potential future clients.

But Nvidia directed all that coverage to Side A only, according to CNBC's source. Side A protects directors and officers personally when the company cannot indemnify them. Side B covers the company for legal defense costs or settlements on behalf of directors and officers, and Side C protects the company when it's named as a defendant in a suit such as a securities claim.

The risk advisor says Nvidia believed it had "the war chest" to protect itself against a securities class action suit.

That choice is raising questions about whether the board protected itself at the company’s expense. CNBC asked Nvidia for comment but received no response.

An insurance CEO characterized a billion-dollar policy as a lot of coverage, but said a Side A-only allocation was a surprising move because it results in imbalanced coverage, protecting only directors.

That structure is not automatically a governance failure, according to a D&O insurance expert with long experience in coverage for banks, drugmakers and other businesses that often face litigation. Side A-only programs are common among companies with the capital to manage the corporate risk internally.

"For a company with Nvidia’s resources, retaining the company-side risk can make financial sense," the advisor said. It's Side A D&O that's "imperative to corporate governance."

"It is a capital-allocation decision," the expert told me. The company decides that buying insurance for its own balance sheet is not worth the premium. In other words, Side B and Side C are considered too expensive for the coverage the company gets.

The question for shareholders is whether the board’s decision to hold that risk was a sound use of the company’s resources and whether the company can absorb the costs if the claims grow.

A shareholder derivative complaint filed Nov. 11 names Huang, directors and other officers. It alleges that they failed to oversee risks involving Huang’s relationship with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang and made misleading statements. It also alleges that some defendants sold roughly $2 billion in Nvidia stock while holding material nonpublic information. Those remain allegations, not findings.

A separate securities class action, filed Nov. 9, names Nvidia and Huang. It seeks damages for investors who bought Nvidia shares between Oct. 9, 2025, and Nov. 8, 2026, alleging the company and Huang misled investors.

The distinction matters: The derivative suit is brought on Nvidia’s behalf, while the class action seeks recovery for investors.

"Insurance is already at work," says Michel Léonard, chief economist at the Insurance Information Institute, describing standard policy mechanics, not Nvidia’s specific policy. "Once the suit is filed, D&O starts paying defense costs, long before anyone proves anything."

A claim still has to meet the policy’s terms, and defense costs can reduce the remaining limits. Nor does a drop in Nvidia’s market value by itself establish an insurable loss. Plaintiffs would need to prove legally recoverable damages; the policy would respond only to covered losses.

The board has already taken steps it says are aimed at accountability. Nvidia announced an independent investigation on Nov. 8, and independent directors retained outside counsel two days later. Huang resigned as CEO and a director on Nov. 11; the board appointed CFO Colette Kress interim CEO. Nvidia said it had no reason to believe national security or company secrets had been compromised by Huang's extramarital relationships.

Atkins, who joined the board of Wynn Resorts in 2018 after founder Steve Wynn resigned, argues that allegations are not conclusions and that boards should also weigh governance concerns against the value a founder brings to a company’s innovation. Nvidia's investigation is continuing even as Huang resumes leadership.

“Will companies’ hyper-accelerated innovation speed be the same without them? I don’t think so,” said Atkins, author of "Don't Waste a Board Seat: A Decision-Maker's Guide to Choosing Directors Who Create Value."

Nvidia’s 2026 proxy also says the company has indemnity agreements with its directors and officers — separate from its insurance. Those agreements provide for the company to cover certain costs and liabilities when the law permits.

#2711. The clock is ticking on Mike McCarthy's time with the Steelers

When it comes to the nuclear war of words that Aaron Rodgers started on Wednesday, the end result is the same as it would be if the world’s superpowers ever started hunting and pecking the launch codes.

Rodgers, as multiple former Green Bay Packers are making clear, is destroying his reputation and legacy as a teammate by breaking the fundamental code of the locker room. But he’s also destroying Mike McCarthy’s reputation and legacy as a coach.

For a change, Rodgers’s rant was centered in reality. ESPNFL reports that the things Rodgers said about McCarthy are true.

Which could make it impossible for the Steelers to keep McCarthy beyond the 2026 season.

His only path to salvation is to win. Starting on Friday, when the 8-2 Broncos come to town for a game against a Steelers team that, despite the sudden dysfunction, is 6-4.

It’s really that simple. The next seven games will become the litmus test as to whether McCarthy’s now-documented snoring-and-ice-cream-sandwiches flaws are outweighed by his capabilities.

Of course, the fact that Rodgers rolled a grenade into the locker room on his way out won’t make that any easier. Which could be one of the reasons why Rodgers did it.

Maximum chaos will make it harder for McCarthy to win. Which will make it harder for McCarthy to make it to Year 2. Which will create the impression that Rodgers has been vindicated.

Sure, the initial word is that the situation doesn’t impact McCarthy’s standing. But the most important aspect of Wednesday’s report from ESPNFL that McCarthy “has the full support of the organization” carries an important qualifier.

The Steelers are “not planning to make any immediate changes.”

So they’re not firing McCarthy or asking him to resign before Friday’s game. What happens if the Steelers lose by double digits to the Broncos? What happens if the current two-game losing streak becomes an extended skid that sweeps them out of the AFC postseason field?

The answer will become obvious based on how the final seven games unfold. In the immediate aftermath of Aaron Rodgers dumping Agent Orange on the organization, it’s hard to imagine McCarthy surviving this.

Ultimately, the decision will be made by owner Art Rooney II. And the outcome could show where the Steelers reside on the line that divides the functional from dysfunctional franchises.

Functional teams admit mistakes and commence rectifying them. Dysfunctional teams deny the facts and double down.

#2710. From Cooper Flagg to Ben Simmons, a look at Montverde Academy’s top NBA draft picks

Montverde Academy (FL) has established itself as one of the premier pipelines for basketball talent in the country, producing NBA stars and some of the sport's most recognizable names.

From No. 1 overall selections to first-round picks who have gone on to become franchise cornerstones, the Central Florida powerhouse has built an impressive résumé at the professional level.

With three players selected first overall in the NBA Draft, here is a look at the 10 highest NBA Draft picks to graduate from Montverde Academy.

The third Montverde Academy product to be selected No. 1 overall, Flagg was the centerpiece of the school's undefeated 2023-24 national championship team. After one season at Duke, he was selected first overall by Dallas in 2025 and won NBA Rookie of the Year in 2026. He is now emerging as the face of the Mavericks' franchise

Cunningham became Montverde's second No. 1 overall selection after leading the Eagles alongside Scottie Barnes and Moses Moody. Following one season at Oklahoma State, he was drafted first overall by Detroit. He has since become a two-time NBA All-Star and led the Pistons' resurgence, including a 60-win season in 2025-26

Simmons became Montverde's first No. 1 overall NBA Draft pick after starring for the Eagles before playing one season at LSU. He won NBA Rookie of the Year in 2018 and became a three-time All-Star with Philadelphia and Brooklyn. His NBA career has since been derailed by injuries, and he is no longer an established NBA roster player.

Russell helped lead Montverde to a national championship before playing one season at Ohio State. He was selected second overall by the Lakers and has gone on to play for several NBA franchises, including Brooklyn, Golden State, Minnesota and the Lakers.

A former five-star recruit, Barrett starred at Montverde before playing one season at Duke. He was selected third overall by the Knicks and spent four-plus seasons in New York before being traded to Toronto in 2023. He remains a key member of the Raptors.

Barnes was part of Montverde's loaded 2020-21 team alongside Cunningham and Moody. After one season at Florida State, he was selected fourth overall by Toronto. He won NBA Rookie of the Year in 2022 and has since become a two-time All-Star and franchise cornerstone.

Duren spent his final high school season at Montverde before playing one year at Memphis. Originally selected 13th overall by Charlotte, his draft rights were traded to Detroit. He has developed into one of the Pistons' key frontcourt players and earned his first NBA All-Star selection in 2026.

Queen was part of Montverde's undefeated 33-0 national championship team in 2023-24. Following one season at Maryland, he was selected 13th overall by Atlanta before being traded to New Orleans. He is now beginning his NBA career with the Pelicans.

Moody helped Montverde capture a national championship during the 2020-21 season before playing one year at Arkansas. #2709. Kyle Shanahan on Brandon Aiyuk signing with Commanders: "They got a good player"

The Aaron Rodgers rigmarole has pushed plenty of other stories out of the spotlight. Including the sudden second act for Brandon Aiyuk.

Aiyuk visited the Commanders on Wednesday, two days after being released by the 49ers and one day after clearing waivers. He promptly signed with the team’s practice squad.

49ers coach Kyle Shanahan was asked for his thoughts on Aiyuk landing with the Commanders.

“None,” Shanahan told reporters. “It was just a transactional thing and it’s good for Washington. They got a good player.”

Indeed they did. That’s why the 49ers signed him to a four-year, $120 million contract only 27 months ago. They could have traded him to the Steelers. They paid him.

It all fell apart after that, perhaps fueled by the lingering rancor of the protracted and contentious contract talks. Everyone hopefully learned a lesson.

Now, the Commanders have a much-needed piece to the offense. A player who can help fill the void created when Terry McLaurin was lost for the season.

And the Commanders — despite being 4-5-1 — remain in solid position to make a late-season run. With seven games to play, they’re two games behind the Giants. The Commanders hold the tiebreaker, thanks to the 1-0-1 record in their 2026 head-to-head competition.

The Commanders face the Cardinals, Titans, Texans, Falcons, Vikings, Jaguars, and Cowboys. The Giants have the Colts, 49ers, Seahawks, Browns, Lions, Cowboys, and Eagles.

Along the way, the Commanders will also need to leapfrog the 5-6 Cowboys.

Still, it’s far from crazy to think the Commanders can pull it off.

However it plays out, the Commanders have added a player who will potentially help them navigate the remaining schedule in a way that vaults them into the postseason.

Who knows? Maybe Aiyuk will get a chance to return to Santa Clara in January. And maybe the Commanders will get a chance to do what they nearly did in Week 6.

That’s still weeks away. But it will be here quickly. And Commanders-49ers is one of the various potential permutations that could play out as the playoffs approach and the postseason commences.

#2706. After his Pittsburgh exit, what's next for Aaron Rodgers?

As Aaron Rodgers enters waivers, the first question is whether any team will claim the balance of his one-year contract.

Obviously, no one will do it without ensuring that Rodgers actually wants to play for that team. Unless, of course, a team or two hopes to troll Rodgers by forcing him to show up to play where he doesn’t want to play. Like Marty Schottenheimer did to Deion Sanders in 2002.

So, yes, it would be hilarious if the Jets decide to put in the proper paperwork.

The more likely outcome is that he’ll clear waivers and become a free agent. It will give him the ability to sign with any team, at any time.

No clear-cut contender currently needs a starter. And it would make no sense for Rodgers to sidle up to a quarterback-needy also-ran, like the Cardinals.

Some have suggested that Rodgers could join the Patriots, who will be missing Drake Maye while they try to parlay 5-5 into playoff position. His August comments about the Mike Vrabel-Diana Russini situation would potentially be an impediment to that outcome.

There’s a spicy possibility of Rodgers aligning with the Ravens, who still play the Steelers twice. Is he that petty? At this point, it’s impossible to say he’s not.

Rodgers’s best play could be to wait. Let fate decide. Last year, Broncos quarterback Bo Nix broke his ankle late in a playoff win over the Bills. If Denver’s instant desperation caused them to consider dusting off Drew Brees (despite the fact that he can’t throw a football with his dominant arm), they would have surely called Rodgers, if he’d been available.

Something like that can happen again. Of course, a team that loses its starter to injury between now and the Super Bowl would have to want to do business with him. Which means accepting the very strong possibility that, in time, Rodgers will have grievances to air about his experience.

Because if it goes poorly, it won’t be his fault. There will be other reasons for his struggles. Reasons that he has shown he has no qualms about sharing in his national-media safe space.

During his 22-year career, Rodgers has played for three NFL teams. He ended up disgruntled in each location. If he adds a fourth franchise to the list, he’ll likely find a way to be disgruntled there, too.

Unless it’s a very short-term arrangement. As short as one or two playoff games.

#2705. Observations after Sixers' 5-game win streak ends with blowout loss to Blazers

Observations after Sixers' 5-game win streak ends with blowout loss to Blazers originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers' five-game winning streak was snapped Monday night by the Trail Blazers.

With a 128-111 defeat at Xfinity Mobile Arena, the Sixers dropped their first game of the year against Western Conference opposition and fell to 14-4. Portland improved to 11-6.

LeBron James had a season-high 23 points and six rebounds. Tyrese Maxey scored 22 points and Jaylen Brown added 20.

Deni Avdija led the Blazers with 31 points and seven assists. Donovan Clingan posted 15 points and 18 rebounds.

The Sixers were missing Joel Embiid (illness). Ja Morant (left hamstring strain) and Shaedon Sharpe (right knee meniscus surgery) were among Portland's sidelined players.

Next on the Sixers' schedule is a Wednesday night game vs. the Heat. Here are observations on their blowout loss to the Blazers:

Jabari Walker, listed at 6-foot-7, defied conventional wisdom by winning the opening tip-off against the 7-2 Cllingan. Maxey then canned a three-pointer.

Brown scored the Sixers' next four points with a pair of free throws and a short jumper. VJ Edgecombe's layup gave the team a 9-2 lead. Brown and Dean Wade both returned Monday after sitting out the last two games with left hamstring injuries.

Avdija got hot in the first quarter. He scored 11 quick points, made his first four field goals and helped the Blazers avoid a serious early deficit.

The Sixers took a 32-30 edge with 9.3 seconds left in the first when Walker jammed in a put-back dunk. The former Portland second-round draft pick played 17 minutes in his second start of the season and continued to look deserving of a rotation spot. He posted 10 points and five rebounds.

Adem Bona was available again following an eight-game absence with a cervical spine sprain. However, Dominick Barlow checked in first to back up Walker.

Barlow had an outstanding start to his night. He scored a clever lefty push shot over Clingan and threw down a dunk in the first quarter. Barlow also made a highlight defensive play in his opening stint, defending Avdija in isolation and rejecting his layup attempt.

Bona then subbed in for Barlow with 3:23 left in the first quarter. He had a positive first possession, grabbing an offensive rebound and driving in for a dunk.

Wade later played at center, too. Barlow logged 16 minutes and had six points. Bona recorded four points and two boards in five minutes. Sixers head coach Nick Nurse ended up using a 10-man rotation and did not play rookie guard Labaron Philon Jr. until fourth-quarter garbage time.

Overall, the Sixers' defense remained considerably worse without Embiid. The team also conceded 15 offensive rebounds, including five to Clingan.

"I think your rim protection and ability to do that with some size is always a focal point of being really good defensively," Nurse said. "And then you've got to do it a little bit by committee (with Embiid out). I thought, for the most part, I was looking at possessions where I liked our help into the paint. They were doing a good job of zinging it out.

"I didn't particularly like our (defense) back out. … There were a couple of times they missed those and still got rebounds. We were compacted in the lane with everybody because we didn't get back out, and then still giving up an offensive rebound as well. That's just playing through the possession, a little bit of energy, all that kind of stuff. … We just didn't do enough pieces well."

Brown delivered tons of efficient offense for the Sixers in the first half and sure didn't appear rusty. His layup late in the second quarter tied the game at 58-all. The five-time All-Star scored 19 first-half points on 8-for-10 shooting.

Avdija exceeded Brown's production, hitting heat-check threes, leaners through contact and just about everything he put up regardless of the defender. He tallied 25 points in the first half and shot 9 for 12 from the field.

James reached 16 points when he capped a high-scoring half by nailing a corner three. The contest was even at 69 apiece heading into halftime.

Monday's game was James' first of the season with three or more made three-pointers. The four-time MVP went 4 for 5 beyond the arc. He'd gone 10 for 46 (21.7 percent) over his first 13 games and was due for a good long-range night.

James was whistled for his third foul early in the third quarter. Brown picked up his fourth with 10:15 to go in the period, forcing him to sit for an extended stretch.

"I wasn't too happy about it. … I think that affected the game," Brown said. "It also affected my rhythm a little bit in the second half. I had to sit (almost) the whole third quarter. Coming back from injury, coming back from a hamstring thing, my body didn't really feel the same after that."

Brown noted postgame that he had "a little bit of soreness and stuff like that."

"I think everything will check out," he said. "The medical staff is on top of everything. Those hamstrings are tricky, so you want to make sure you play it the right way, be safe. I also don't want to miss a lot of games, so I might be out there, but I've also got to be smart. I think I played it the right way today."

Avdija stopped lighting up the Sixers in the third period, but the team still had another unimpressive defensive quarter. Portland posted 32 points in the third and built its lead to double figures in the opening minute of the fourth.

The game devolved into a blowout. An Avdija dunk put the Blazers' advantage at 22 points with 5:15 on the clock and the Sixers didn't have a miracle comeback in store.

Even with all their wins, there's no question the Sixers have been trending downward on defense over the past couple of weeks, allowing regular dribble penetration and plenty of comfortable threes.

They'll aim to raise their level on that side of the floor and expect Embiid's presence to be a major help once he's back in action.

"I think it's just mindset," Walker said. "We're capable when we want to. You need games like this every now and then just to remind you that it's not as easy as it feels sometimes. It takes effort every game.

"I think we can learn a lot from this. It's just part of the growing pains, but I'm confident we'll get back to that (early-season) level of defense. We have what it takes."

#2704. Five matchups that will decide Eagles vs. Cowboys

The Philadelphia Eagles will face several difficult personnel matchups when they travel to AT&T Stadium for Thursday's Thanksgiving game against the Dallas Cowboys. Dallas generated explosive plays through the air and rushed for 155 yards with Javonte Williams during its 38-21 victory over Philadelphia in October.

The rematch presents opportunities for the Eagles on both sides of the ball, particularly against a Dallas defense allowing 151.5 rushing yards per game.

Here are five matchups that could determine the outcome.

Kendall will have his hands full against one of the NFL's most disruptive interior defensive linemen.

Williams' combination of power and quickness can create problems for centers and guards, and Philadelphia's ability to handle him without consistently committing multiple blockers will impact its running game and Joe Milton's opportunities from the pocket.

Pickens scored on a 21-yard touchdown reception against Philadelphia in Week 7 and presents a difficult matchup because of his size, ability to track the deep ball and effectiveness in contested-catch situations.

Mitchell's availability and Woolen's performance on the outside will be critical.

Lamb's versatility allows Dallas to create favorable matchups through motion and different personnel groupings.

DeJean's ability to play multiple positions gives Vic Fangio some flexibility, while Kenny Moore II offers another experienced defender capable of handling slot responsibilities.

Bell faces another developmental test against a proven NFL pass rusher who can win with power.

Dallas can also rotate Von Miller, James Houston and Donovan Ezeiruaku, ensuring Bell sees different styles of pass rushers throughout the afternoon.

Philadelphia cannot allow Williams to dictate the game as he did in October. Davis and Carter must control the interior, prevent Dallas from creating clean rushing lanes and force Prescott into more predictable passing situations.

#2702. On Our Way Home is free on Thursday and Friday

The holiday season is here. And I’m in the mood to give something away. (It must be the whiskey.)

The On Our Way Home ebook is available for free on Thursday and Friday.

Why not give something away? This is the week when everyone is trying to sell you something. No one is giving you anything, with zero strings attached.

On Our Way Home is primarily a Christmas story. It’s also a ghost story. I cranked it out between Thanksgiving and New Year’s Day a few years back.

In the interests of avoiding any spoilers, I’ll just say this: Download it and give it a try. It’s essentially about family and redemption and reconciliation. It’s also about forgiving others, while finding a way to forgive yourself.

It’s funny at times. It’s sad at times. If you make it to the end, you’ll possibly shed a tear or two.

The best feedback I’ve gotten came from a reader who had suffered from PTSD for years. Reading On Our Way Home unlocked his ability to feel emotions again.

I never intended anything like that. I just had an idea for a story, years before writing it. One year, I got caught up in the spirit of the season and it flowed, one chapter, one page, one word at a time.

The price is right. If you don’t like it, delete it. If you like it, keep going.

Speaking of free, Quarterback of the Future is being posted, one chapter at a time. Twenty-five chapters are up. A new one is coming every day until it’s done.

Someone asked recently why my break from writing consists of more writing. There’s something magical and, frankly, fun about creating something out of nothing. It’s even more fun when people read it and enjoy it.

Whether you enjoy it is up to you. If you don’t, that’s on me. But it won’t cost you a penny to find out, if you download On Our Way Home on Thursday or Friday.

The Pittsburgh Steelers have elevated offensive lineman Doug Nester from the practice squad for the second straight week for the team's Week 12 Black Friday game against the Denver Broncos.

Nester will again replace guard Mason McCormick, who suffered a gruesome leg injury in the Steelers' Week 10 loss to the Cincinnati Bengals.

A native of Kenya, West Virginia, first attended Virginia Tech for his first two collegiate seasons before transferring to WVU. Nester started 10 games as a true freshman at right guard for the Hokies in 2019 and seven more in 2020. After transferring to West Virginia, he stated every game in 2021 and 2022 at right guard, before moving to right tackle for his redshirt senior season in 2023. Steelers guard Doug Nester during an OTAs practice on May 29, 2025. — Ed Thompson / Steelers Now

#2700. Semiconductor chips are the new oil. Here's why

The artificial intelligence boom has pushed semiconductors past oil and gas in global export value for the first time, according to a Deutsche Bank analysis of International Trade Centre data.

Yet the milestone arrives at an awkward moment, just as investors reassess the outlook for artificial intelligence spending and drive down the price of semiconductor stocks. Last week, before Monday's breathtaking reversal, semiconductor stocks suffered their worst weekly loss in a quarter century, with the PHLX Semiconductor Index (SOX) plunging nearly 11% last Friday alone, capping a more than 17% weekly decline.

Nvidia soared more than 31% Monday after the leading maker of artificial intelligence chips had fallen for a seventh straight week, plunging 46% during that stretch. Then it fell again, dropping almost 10% on Tuesday and Wednesday. Advanced Micro Devices tumbled 20% in two days last Thursday and Friday. Micron Technology sank 27% over the seven days ended last Friday.

"For decades we've talked about the petrodollar. Perhaps increasingly we need to think about the chip dollar," Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research at Deutsche Bank wrote in a report this month.

Semiconductor exports overtook oil and gas for the first time during the January-March quarter of 2026, reaching about $1.61 trillion, compared with $1.53 trillion for oil and gas, the report said, using four-quarter rolling totals.

The gap widened in the second quarter, when semiconductor exports totaled about $1.60 trillion and oil and gas exports reached about $1.47 trillion. Disruptions to oil supplies through the Strait of Hormuz after the Iran war helped widen the gap. Daily oil flows through the Strait collapsed nearly 77%, to 4.9 million barrels in the second quarter of 2026 from 21.6 million barrels in the fourth quarter of 2025, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

Yet the demand for semiconductors has proven insatiable in the face of soaring data center construction, boosting global trade in the increasingly scarce AI component. Hundreds of billions of dollars of orders for graphics processing units and data centers aim at providing AI computing power, Rothschild & Co. Redburn wrote in a report last Thursday.

"Compute will be the new commodity fueling this transformation on a global scale," Rothschild analyst Cara Thomson said.

The shift toward chips has macroeconomic implications just as the explosion in oil trade did in the 1970s.

Oil-exporting countries historically recycled much of their surpluses into the purchase of U.S. Treasuries and other bonds, helping finance U.S. deficits and underpin demand for other government debt.

Reid at Deutsche Bank said that since semiconductor-surplus countries in Asia are more closely tied to U.S. tech companies, some chip-export earnings could flow back into U.S. technology stocks, startups and data centers, further helping to finance the AI investment cycle.

The changing dynamics in global trade could also tilt the mix of global financial flows, Reid said. "So welcome to the chip-dollar era: potentially more growth, more excitement, more volatility, and structurally higher yields" in corporate and government debt.

Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers stayed unbeaten Saturday night at Xfinity Mobile Arena, earning a 127-116 win over the Bucks and improving to 3-0 on the season.

Joel Embiid had his 10th career regular-season triple-double, tallying 28 points, 11 rebounds and 10 assists.

On his 30th birthday, Jaylen Brown posted 27 points and five assists. Tyrese Maxey had 26 points. VJ Edgecombe scored 17 and grabbed 13 boards.

The Sixers' absences on the first night of a back-to-back included LeBron James (low back/sciatica management). Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said pregame that he did not know yet who would be available for his team's matchup with the Pistons on Sunday.

Here are observations on the Sixers' victory Saturday:

Dean Wade made his Sixers debut and started in James' place. He'd missed the first two games of the regular season with a left ankle sprain.

The 3-and-D forward scored the night's first points by a sinking a corner three-pointer on the opening possession.

Embiid also had a sharp start. He moved well, made good decisions and served as the main hub of his team's offense in the early going.

The Sixers' seven-time All-Star center has often enjoyed facing Myles Turner. He entered the night with an average of 29.4 points in 18 previous games against the Bucks big man.

Embiid did a little bit of everything in the first quarter, posting eight points, four assists and four rebounds over nine minutes. After snatching an offensive board, Embiid drained a fadeaway jumper to give the Sixers a 10-1 lead.

One of Embiid's assists was quite stylish. He found Edgecombe open beyond the arc with a behind-the-back bounce pass. Edgecombe knocked down the shot and wound up going 3 for 4 from three-point range in the first quarter.

The Sixers added rookie Labaron Philon Jr. to their rotation. Jabari Walker stayed in the mix, though he didn't enter until the 7:36 mark of the second quarter.

Philon played four minutes in his NBA debut and missed his lone shot attempt, a corner three. On defense, Philon allowed a couple of blow-bys off the dribble. He generally looked like he belonged on offense, albeit without any production in his brief run.

Maxey banked in a half-court heave at the first-quarter buzzer to put the Sixers up nine points. The Sixers couldn't carry forward any momentum, however, and began the second quarter poorly.

Adem Bona had another rough stint amid a subpar start to the season. After Anfernee Simons missed a transition layup try, Ryan Rollins' three lifted the Bucks into a 40-37 lead.

The dreadful stretch for the Sixers on both sides of the ball called to mind how they'd fallen into a 29-point deficit Thursday night vs. the Cavaliers before clawing out a comeback win.

The Sixers mustered just seven points in first six minutes of the second quarter and had many stagnant possessions that concluded with contested jumpers. The team's transition defense was dismal for much of the second period. Milwaukee had the game's first 19 fast-break points.

The Sixers regained the lead late in the second quarter. Kentavious Caldwell-Pope made two three-balls in the second and nabbed three first-half steals. Embiid assisted a go-ahead, and-one Walker layup.

Brown hit a three with 11.8 seconds left in the second quarter. Unsurprisingly, his variety of shotmaking skills were useful without James in the lineup.

Even when James or Embiid sit, the Sixers should have a simple advantage in terms of volume of stars over most opponents this year. None of Brown, Embiid or Maxey had the sort of off night that would have improved the Bucks' odds of a road win. They'd all passed the 20-point mark by the end of the third quarter.

Maxey notched another final-possession bucket, this time with a more conventional make. He canned a jumper from the right elbow with 1.7 seconds left in the third to extend the Sixers' lead to 97-87.

The Bucks made a late push in the fourth quarter. Kel'el Ware's put-back, and-one layup cut the Milwaukee's deficit to 117-114.

The Sixers ultimately handled business. Embiid reached his triple-double by assisting a second-chance Brown jumper and and Caldwell-Pope soon drilled a dagger corner three. Embiid even threw down a last-minute dunk for good measure.

For the second consecutive season, the Sixers have a 3-0 start. They got to four wins last year before dropping their first game.

#2694. Blake Corum supplants Kyren Williams as the Rams' top tailback

It’s been slowly building throughout the season. On Wednesday night, it became abundantly clear.

Blake Corum has become the Rams’ top tailback.

On his 26th birthday, Corum had a career night. Thirty-two carries, 184 yards, and a touchdown. Throw in 21 receiving yards, and he had 205 yards from scrimmage.

“Happy birthday, man,” coach Sean McVay told reporters after the game. “He was on the set of Netflix so we didn’t even get to enjoy it with him. So, I know that kind of pissed me off, honestly.”

Corum’s gains have come at the expense of Kyren Williams. Despite a report that he’s been dealing with turf toe for a month, this week was Williams’s first appearance all year on the injury report.

And while the fact that Corum got the start last night and 58 snaps while Williams was limited to 38 may have had something to do with the toe, as Mike Tomlin says, “One man’s misfortune is another man’s opportunity.”

Corum seized the opportunity on Wednesday night, as part of a very un-Rams-like offensive output that included 241 rushing yards and 132 passing yards.

For the season, Williams has 662 rushing yards and an average of 4.4 yards per carry. Corum has 731 yards rushing with a 5.4-yard average.

Lurking in the background (but soon moving to the foreground) is the business side of the situation. Corum is in the third year of a slotted, third-round rookie deal. He’s making $1.582 million in 2026, and he’s eligible for a second contract as soon as the regular season ends.

Williams is making $11 million per year, on a deal that runs through 2028.

They’ll need to reward Corum at some point, which could force them to make a decision about Williams.

That’s clearly coming. Last night’s breakout showing in a standalone game shows that it’s coming quickly.

#2693. LeBron Log No. 6: A Rocky night, a shooting lesson and a fight over ‘Bron'

LeBron Log No. 6: A Rocky night, a shooting lesson and a fight over 'Bron' originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

It was another eventful week for LeBron James.

That's why we started the LeBron Log in the first place.

The King spent his latest week taking his teammates to the movies, fighting over his name in federal court and producing his best three-point shooting performance as a Sixer days after recording a podcast about the craft.

This week also marks 20 years since James faced the Sixers alongside Allen Iverson.

James found an appropriate choice for the Sixers' latest team outing.

He organized a private screening of I Play Rocky on Friday night for players, their families and members of the basketball operations staff. The film follows Sylvester Stallone's fight to get the original Rocky made while insisting that he play the title character.

"I mean, it's Rocky. We in Philly," James said. "I heard it was a great movie, and we had a night off. I've got a few connections, and I was able to bring that to my teammates and this organization for us to watch it. I thought it was a great movie. Unbelievably cast. Everyone looked like exactly who they were portraying. That is Hollywood for you. It was pretty cool."

The Sixers shared photos of James alongside Jaylen Brown, Kentavious Caldwell-Pope, Labaron Philon Jr., Jabari Walker, Tacko Fall and Adem Bona.

"Movie night, courtesy of LeBron," the team wrote.

The nationwide release of I Play Rocky came less than two weeks before Philadelphia celebrates the 50th anniversary of the original film on Dec. 3.

Nick Nurse could not attend because of a previous commitment, but he received positive reviews from his players.

"They went, they said it was very good, they loved it," Nurse said. "The big takeaway was how much Anthony actually looked like Rocky. Or Sylvester Stallone. One in the same."

James' first season in Philadelphia now includes a private Rocky screening. A trip up the Art Museum steps remains available for a future edition.

James and Steve Nash devoted the latest episode of their Mind the Game podcast to the art of shooting.

The two examined shooting form, confidence, repetitions, free throws and some of their favorite jumpers. James also revealed one detail that can affect what he does after catching the ball.

"I'm a guy who don't like shooting against the laces," James said. "So sometimes I'll come up on a quick stop and I'm about to raise and I can feel the laces not fixed. I'll turn that into a pump fake."

The episode was released Nov. 17, while James was experiencing an extended struggle from three-point range. It did not provide an instant fix.

James went 1 for 5 from three against Orlando and missed his lone attempt against Milwaukee. He entered Monday night's meeting with Portland shooting 21.7 percent from deep through his first 13 games.

James made all three of his first-half attempts from three. He ended the second quarter by pump-faking, stepping to his left and beating the buzzer with a corner three that tied the game at 69.

Nobody could see where the laces sat on the catch. The pump fake was clear.

James finished 4 for 5 from three and scored a season-high 23 points on 8-for-13 shooting. It was his third consecutive game with at least 20 points, following 22 against Orlando and 21 against Milwaukee.

The Sixers lost to Portland, 128-111, but James produced his best long-range performance since joining them.

Six days after discussing the art of shooting, he provided a brief demonstration.

James is also attempting to protect one of his most recognizable nicknames.

James and LBJ Trademarks LLC filed a federal lawsuit on Nov. 17 against PlayVision Inc. and its founders over a sports-betting research app initially called "Bron."

The complaint alleges that the company used an AI-generated version of James in an advertisement without his permission. The figure wore a No. 23 jersey with "Bron" across the back and resembled James through its voice, build and tattoos.

It also scrolled through wagers involving NBA players.

The lawsuit alleges that the advertisement falsely created the impression that James endorsed the app and suggested that he considered betting on NBA games. The complaint said the video received roughly 1 million views before it was removed.

"The integrity of NBA competition, and the public's confidence that players are not betting on the games they play, is of paramount importance to the league, its players and its fans," the complaint said. "Any suggestion that an active NBA player is betting on NBA games is therefore far from a trivial matter, and it should not be used for clicks and views."

The app offered odds comparisons, betting trends and tracking tools but did not directly accept wagers, according to its developer.

PlayVision renamed it "Evie" on Nov. 18, one day after James filed the lawsuit. James is seeking an injunction and unspecified damages. The case remains active in the Southern District of New York.

CLEVELAND – NOVEMBER 25: LeBron James #23 of the Cleveland Cavaliers looks to pass off when double teamed by the Philadelphia 76ers November 25, 2006 at The Quicken Loans Arena in Cleveland, Ohio. Copyright 2006 NBAE (Photo by David Liam Kyle/NBAE via Getty Images)

James spent Thanksgiving weekend in 2006 on the other side of the Sixers-Cavaliers matchup.

On Nov. 25, 2006, a 21-year-old James recorded 25 points, 11 assists, four rebounds and one block in Cleveland's 108-95 win over Philadelphia.

Donning the Cavs' old-school orange threads, he played nearly 41 minutes.

Iverson led the Sixers with 31 points. Andre Iguodala added 17 points and eight rebounds, while Kyle Korver made three three-pointers off the bench.

James recorded 11 assists that night. Nearly 20 years later, another 11-assist performance against Indiana moved him past Jason Kidd for third place in NBA history.

The 2006 meeting also came near the end of Iverson's original run with Philadelphia. The Sixers traded him to Denver less than a month later.

James was 21. Iverson was nearing his departure.

Twenty years later, James is wearing a Sixers uniform and Iverson's No. 3 hangs above his home floor.

#2690. Art Rooney II expresses support for Mike McCarthy, calls Aaron Rodgers not a "good teammate"

After Wednesday’s unprecedented chaos, it had to happen. And it did.

Steelers owner Art Rooney II has addressed the events that resulted in the benching and then the firing of quarterback Aaron Rodgers.

“A change had to be made, and I certainly agree with the change and the way it was handled,” Rooney told Gerry Dulac of the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette in a Thursday interview.

The change was sparked by the notion that Rodgers gave coach Mike McCarthy an ultimatum: “Either let me call all the plays or just release me.” Instead, McCarthy benched him.

It went to the next level when, as many expected, Rodgers scurried to the McAfee show to take shots at McCarthy for missing meetings, showing up late to meetings, and falling asleep in meetings — among other things, including the ultra-embarrassing “1-2-3 Packers!” moment from halftime of Sunday’s loss to the Eagles.

“There’s maybe a time and place after the season if he wanted to kind of unload,” Rooney said. “He talks about wanting to be a good teammate, but you don’t do that to your teammates a couple days before the game, that’s for sure. . . .

“In general, I think, historically, what’s in the locker room stays in the locker room. That’s the way it’s always been. That’s the way it should be as far as I’m concerned.”

Rooney also confirmed that the team supports McCarthy, despite Rodgers’s rant and reports confirming the facts underpinning the petty delivery of them.

“I just want to say that I have 100 [percent] confidence in Mike McCarthy and I expect he’ll be our coach this season, next season and beyond,” Rooney told Dulac. “The big thing, what happened this week, is insubordination can’t be tolerated in any organization. When you start getting ultimatums, you can’t live with that.”

Rooney also was asked whether Rodgers raised with the owner supposed concerns about McCarthy’s health.

“Nothing,” Rooney said. “Mike’s as healthy as the rest of us. Health was not an issue. I’m not sure where that part comes [from].”

Rooney also addressed something that has been largely overlooked during the fast-moving drama: Rodgers’s subpar performance.

“The sad thing is Mike took some of the bullets for Aaron in terms of some of the plays that were called, particularly in the red-zone troubles that we had,” Rooney said. “Mike took some of the bullets for things that were going wrong down there. He tried to protect him, and it just wasn’t working.”

They should have known it wouldn’t work between Rodgers and McCarthy. It’s still unclear why either one of them thought it would. McCarthy shouldn’t have wanted a reunion with Rodgers. And Rodgers shouldn’t have wanted a second act with McCarthy.

Then again, it’s not as if Rodgers had many choices. In 2025, he had few takers. In 2026, he had fewer. If he was going to ensure that his final NFL throw wasn’t a pick-six by playing another year, Pittsburgh wasn’t just the best place.

#2684. James can still take over ‘any given moment,' and Sixers trust he'll pick right spots

James can still take over 'any given moment,' and Sixers trust he'll pick right spots originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

LeBron James isn't oblivious to the calendar and the clock.

He knows he'll turn 42 years old next month, he's ancient by NBA standards and decline is inevitable.

James also knows who he is and what he still can do, whatever the norms are for players of a certain age.

"I think his battle against Father Time is one of the most impressive things he's done over the course of his entire career," Heat head coach Erik Spoelstra said Wednesday before Miami's loss to the Sixers. "We all know and everybody always says that Father Time always wins. But right now he's giving Father Time hell."

James went on to record his first triple-double with the 15-4 Sixers, posting 25 points, 12 assists and 10 rebounds. The four-time MVP is at 126 regular-season triple-doubles and counting in his career.

Only Russell Westbrook, Nikola Jokic, Oscar Robertson and Magic Johnson have more in NBA history. James is 17 above Philadelphia native and Sixers legend Wilt Chamberlain.

With Joel Embiid sidelined by illness for a second consecutive game and Jaylen Brown ruled out at halftime with left hamstring tightness, James' do-it-all performance was timely. Tyrese Maxey's 30-point, six-assist outing was essential, too.

"I'm just trying to play the game the right way," James said. "I don't think my job is to dominate the game every night for this ball club. We have a Finals MVP (Brown), we have a regular-season MVP (Embiid), we have an up-and-coming superstar at point guard, we've got a young fella in VJ (Edgecombe) who's up and coming as well.

"My dues are paid with what I've done. If they need me to dust off the cape from time to time, then I can still accomplish that. But that's not my job. … But if they need it, I can do it at any given moment."

James' night featured a flurry of very deep three-pointers in the second quarter.

He started the season 10 for 46 beyond the arc (21.7 percent), but his percentage has risen to 31.6 with two sweet-shooting games in a row.

"The work has been put in and I'm not ever worried about anything as far as my game," he said. "The difference between the start of the season and now is that my legs are feeling better, my ramp-up is feeling better.

"I'm about to be 42 years old in a month. S—, it takes a little bit longer for the ramp-up, but I've been feeling pretty good as of late. I don't ever second-guess myself … because I know the work that I put in."

While James' rebounding was perhaps the least spectacular aspect of his game, Sixers head coach Nick Nurse appreciated his work on the boards.

James has remained a statistically solid defensive rebounder into his 40s and he's one reason why the Sixers have made a major improvement in that department. According to Cleaning the Glass, the Sixers' opponents have grabbed 28.4 percent of their own misses, which ranks sixth in the NBA. The team ranked 27th last season.

Asked about James' cape comments, Maxey shouted out, "Dust it off then!" with a grin.

Maxey's not sure exactly when James will dramatically elevate his game, but he trusts the 22-time All-Star to pick the right spots.

"I don't know," Maxey said. "Early in the game, he was telling me he was tired. I said, 'Well, we don't have time for you to be tired.'

"But he does a good job of just managing the game. He knows when he needs to score, he knows when he needs to pass. We're going to need a lot from him. I know he's seasoned, but we expect a lot of him and he does that."

#2679. Why isn’t the Las Vegas Raiders defense good enough

Stop me if you've heard this before, but the Las Vegas Raiders defense has got a lot of growing to do to catch up with the offense. They have come within one score of, or surpassed, the 40-point threshold for the sixth time in 11 games.

Head coach Klint Kubiak said they win as a team and lose as a team; refusing to point fingers is noble and expected of the head coach. Defensive coordinator Rob Leonard elected not to take the high road, instead making a snide comment: "Fatigue makes cowards of us all…when you're on the field a long time, mistakes tend to happen more often." But here, we aren't limited by nobility; Leonard would have gotten a pass until he decided to open his mouth and speak on an offense ranking 29th in time of possession but 6th in total points.

So let us start by looking at who has been truly responsible for this lackluster defense. Leonard is the one calling the defensive plays and maintaining a league-worst defensive efficiency allowed, a paltry 48.1% defensive success rate and a 15.9% explosive play rate.

No one is doing jack up front for the Raiders defensive line outside of Maxx Crosby. Over the last three weeks, the Raiders defensive line has 2.5 sacks, five tackles for loss, seven quarterback hits, 1 forced fumble and two pass breakups. Crosby is the owner of every single one of those stats except one quarterback hit from Kwity Paye, Malcolm Koonce and Tonka Hemingway, along with the 0.5 sack, forced fumble and two pass breakups that Folorunso Fatukasi has produced.

Kwity Paye, a high-priced free agent acquisition, hasn't had a sack since Week 6 at home against the Buffalo Bills. Coincidentally, that happened to be the date of his last tackle for loss as well. His last quarterback hit was against Brock Purdy in Week 9. Hardly worthy of his lofty three-year, $48 million ($16 million average) contract.

Cutting him with a June-1 designation saves roughly $6.01 million, with $16.824 million (one year's salary) dead cap. At the rate of one sack every 5-6 weeks, one quarterback hit roughly every 2-3 weeks and a tackle for loss every six weeks, the rubber is going to have to meet the road at some point.

Malcolm Koonce, last year Koonce got a pass for coming off an injured knee and was kept over a more deserving K'Lavon Chaisson. After receiving a good-faith one-year $11.01 million contract, his good start to the 2026 season has faded into oblivion along with his productivity. Over the last three games, he has two tackles and a quarterback hit.

This season, he has accounted for 12 tackles, seven quarterback hits, three sacks, two forced fumbles and 1 tackle for loss. His last 0.5 sack was in Week 5 against the New England Patriots; the quarterback hit against the Denver Broncos on Sunday was his first impact as a rusher in six weeks.

Adam Butler, according to Pro Football Focus, ranks 84th out of 134 qualified interior defensive linemen. Strangely enough, Butler's best grade is as a run defender, ranking 49th of 134 and then comes the fall. His 21 total tackles are outside the Top 50 defensive tackles; his 0.5 sacks are outside the Top 75 defensive tackles; his seven total quarterback pressures are in the bottom third of qualifying defensive interiors.

Eric Stokes has played so poorly as of late that it is baffling how he is still starting. At this point, he has been every opponent's favorite target; more so than even the rookies. When he isn't giving up on plays, he is getting beaten like a drum. Stokes is allowing a passer rating of 115.2, making him the 9th-worst cover corner in the league coming out of week 10. What's worse is that number has been steadily climbing over the last three weeks. In weeks 8-10, he posted a passer rating of 116.1. Additionally, when it comes to penalties, he has four accepted pass interference calls resulting in 58 yards; the first being tied for 5th most and the latter being the 5th most in the league. Stokes may have five pass breakups this season, but he still hasn't recorded an interception since week 4 of his rookie season.

Hezekiah Masses, Jermod McCoy, Darien Porter: All three are rookie cornerbacks who must be afforded an opportunity to learn their craft and experience bumps and bruises along the way. Before blaming them for all the explosive plays generated, we have to understand they are being asked to cover for a league-worst 3.0 seconds to throw and 4th-worst in pocket time allowed, 2.72 seconds.

Individually, they have all experienced success in one way, shape, or form. All of these young defensive backs need to get in the weight room and transform their bodies from college to the pros. Getting acclimated to the league is a process and all of these young players have shown promise.

Masses has three interceptions this year but is still searching for a permanent positional home. Slightly undersized, he has the heart of a lion but needs a good NFL strength and development plan in the offseason. Out wide, he has three interceptions, but his productivity in the slot has been an improvement over veteran Taron Johnson, which offers positional versatility.

He is a better man-coverage corner than soft zone but can do both. A ferocious blitzer who can get home when activated but is still too small to be a nickel linebacker. One of the few blemishes has been his ability to hold contain when he's the last defender on the line.

Porter the second-year cornerback, is a bit of an enigma. Unable to keep his starting job locked down from Masses and McCoy, he hasn't been bad and has proven that, if utilized correctly, he can be an asset to the defense. Porter is a converted wide receiver with size, speed and length who specializes in press-man coverage.

However, the main issue is the press-bail and zone technique he is being asked to play is a style which isn't conducive to what he does best. He is a good and willing tackler, better suited to larger, less quick-twitch receivers. Opposite of Stokes, he is the second-best tackler out past the edges.

McCoy, when healthy, has the tools to be the best of the bunch. Watching him stay balanced, controlled and locate the football was a sight for sore eyes. Playing the ball all the way through the catching process and being able to punch the ball out is what the Raiders need. Tackling in the run game was a problem against the Broncos. All in all, for a rookie making his second start, there are some encouraging signs but also plenty of room for improvement.

Enough can't be said about how disappointing the run defense has been. This season, the 16 rushing touchdowns allowed are tied for the most in the league. The Raiders are allowing 149.5 yards per game, ranking 31st, and 4.82 yards per carry, ranking 30th in the league. Surprisingly, the 51 missed tackles are middle of the pack, so the reality is they are getting outmuscled.

Against the Broncos, the Raiders lost three defensive tackles to injury. Whether they are able to play in the Sunday Night Game against the Cleveland Browns remains to be seen. If they are not, the run defense stands to be even worse.

#2678. Observations after James posts triple-double, Sixers beat Heat in NBA Cup

Observations after James posts triple-double, Sixers beat Heat in NBA Cup originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

LeBron James posted his first triple-double as a Sixer on Wednesday night and led his team to a 111-104 win over the Heat at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

James notched his 126th career regular-season triple-double with 25 points, 12 assists and 10 rebounds for the 15-4 Sixers.

Tyrese Maxey scored 30 points and dished out six assists.

Giannis Antetokounmpo recorded 32 points and 14 rebounds for the 10-7 Heat.

The Sixers improved to 2-1 and Miami fell to 2-1 in Eastern Conference Group B of the NBA Cup.

Jaylen Brown was ruled out at halftime with left hamstring tightness. He had six points on 2-for-8 shooting over 17 minutes.

"He'll get some imaging and we'll get the update tomorrow," Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said.

Joel Embiid (illness) missed his second game in a row. The Sixers are set to visit the Pacers on Friday night in their final Cup group game.

"He's ill," Nurse said of Embiid. "I do not know whether he's going to Indiana yet or not. I guess we'll find that out late tomorrow afternoon."

Here are observations on the Sixers' victory over the Heat:

Nurse emphasized pregame that the Sixers needed an improved defensive performance.

"We've got to compete much better at the defensive end than we did Monday (against the Trail Blazers)," he said. "It's as simple as that."

The night did not begin in especially promising fashion on that front. Antetokounmpo powered through Brown and scored inside for the game's first bucket. His transition layup put Miami up 6-0. The Heat scored nine fast-break points in the first six minutes.

As he had Monday in the Sixers' loss to Portland, Jabari Walker started at center. He was among the Sixers who shared the daunting defensive assignment of Antetokounmpo.

Walker took a charge on the 10-time All-Star in the first quarter, but Antetounkmpo had a stellar start. He forcefully orchestrated Miami's offense, often plowing through the middle of the floor and finding efficient answers.

The Sixers' defense was better late in the first quarter and it didn't hurt when Antetokounmpo took a seat.

Maxey had an aggressive, productive first period, scoring 13 points. Dominick Barlow's tip-in gave the Sixers a 27-26 edge.

James drained three three-pointers early in the second quarter, including a confident, deep jumper that fired up a high-volume home crowd. He's shown that he remains capable of flipping a world-class switch and taking over games in a vast array of ways.

There's no question the 22-time All-Star is out of his early-season outside shooting slump. James has gone 8 for 11 from long range over his last two games. He's scored at least 20 points in four straight.

"I just play the game as it unfolds," James said. "I had a couple of opportunities and I was able to connect on them. I kind of know when my hand is feeling pretty good, especially from the outside. We'll see how long I can keep it going."

Adem Bona checked in early in the second quarter. He provided a string of excellent defensive possessions against Antetokounmpo, including an emphatic block and several well-guarded missed jumpers, although Bona did get called for three fouls in the second period.

Nurse was pleased with what he received defensively from both Bona (two blocks, six rebounds) and Barlow (nine points, eight rebounds) off the bench.

"They used their gifts," he said. "They're quick side to side, both of them. When they're in that kind of fighting mode like that … they did a good job. We tried to get Bona in there when Giannis was in, just for the rim protection. And Dom just played really, really (well) all over the place … on the defense, on the rebounding, on the running, on the cutting."

The Sixers played effective zone defense at the tail end of the second quarter and held a nine-point halftime lead. That grew as high as 16 points in the third quarter.

Miami pulled back within single digits, but the Sixers maintained a healthy advantage and James kept on making highlight plays. He lobbed the ball up to Edgecombe early in the fourth quarter and the second-year guard skied high to lay it in. James later connected with Barlow on an alley-oop.

Once the Sixers have a substantial lead, James' presence is a massive help offensively. He's very well-accustomed to conducting methodical half-court offense, identifying favorable matchups and turning to fruitful actions over and over. James will also still steam forward on the fast break when he sees the chance.

Maxey buried a step-back three to extend his team's lead to 111-95 with 2:29 on the clock and the Sixers polished off a professional win. The fans roared when James snatched the rebound required to reach his triple-double.

"We came out tonight with a different mentality, different energy," Maxey said. "Nurse got on us a little bit in the film (session) yesterday. He lit a fire for a lot of us, which is good. We needed it."

#2674. NFL Black Friday preview: Steelers cut Aaron Rodgers, turn to Mason Rudolph against hot Broncos

Black Friday represents a new dawn for the Pittsburgh Steelers.

The Steelers shockingly benched Aaron Rodgers late Tuesday night, and then released him Wednesday. Pittsburgh faces the 8-2 Denver Broncos at Acrisure Stadium on Friday. It will be Mason Rudolph starting in Rodgers' place for the 6-4 Steelers, who are fighting for their playoff lives after losing two straight since their bye week.

The shock was less because of how Rodgers and the Steelers' offense had played lately — not well — but more so for how the Steelers and head coach Mike McCarthy had backed Rodgers and seemingly endorsed him, as recently as Monday. That all changed when the team benched him, prompting Rodgers to go on ESPN and rip McCarthy while declaring he wouldn't return to the team.

Rodgers reportedly issued McCarthy an ultimatum over total control of play-calling and the head coach declined, and sent the future Hall of Famer on his way in stunning fashion.

Amazingly, it appears as if DK Metcalf will play Friday, less than a week after being ejected from a loss to the Philadelphia Eagles … and it wasn't Metcalf's first such incident. He's amid one of his worst seasons to date and now must match up with Broncos All-Pro CB Pat Surtain II and do so with a backup QB.

Rudolph has seen mop-up action in four games this season. He will make his first start since 2025 against Denver, a team he's never faced. The Broncos have 31 sacks this season, and the Steelers have allowed 31 sacks.

Denver's defense has been closer to good than great this season, but its offense has picked it up after a slow start to the year. In the past four games, the Broncos have scored 26 or more points in each after hitting that mark only once in the first six outings.

The Broncos are riding a six-game win streak and chasing the top playoff seed in the AFC. The Steelers haven't lost at Acrisure this season, but they've failed to hit the 20-point mark in three of their past four games.

The Steelers are in desperation mode. They're currently in the seventh playoff slot and have a 57% chance to make the postseason, according to Next Gen Stats, as things stand right now. That might sound pretty good, and no team currently outside the playoff field is over 50%.

A loss would drop the Steelers' chances to 50%. A win would push them to 72%. Pittsburgh's next four games are against teams still fighting for the postseason.

It's not as if Denver has nothing to play for. It is currently the No. 2 seed in the playoff slotting, just one game behind the Bills, whom the Broncos host in Week 16 on Christmas. The difference between the top seed (which comes with a bye) and the next spot down feels massive.

But the Broncos are near-certainties to make the playoffs, currently sitting at 99% chances to get in. A loss would drop them all the way down to 98%. Their schedule prior to and after the Bills game is soft. It would be tough to lose to a team making a QB change in a short week, but it wouldn't damage Denver's playoff hopes much at all.

Since coming off injured reserve four games ago, Coleman has seen his share of the Broncos' backfield duty increase with each game. On Sunday against the Raiders, the rookie scored three TDs and ran for 111 yards for his best outing of his short NFL career.

The Broncos likely want to see what more Coleman can do, especially with J.K. Dobbins suspended for this game. Perhaps not coincidentally, during Coleman's strong four-game span, Bo Nix and Denver's passing game have produced four straight games with 200-plus passing yards.

The Steelers rank third in rushing yards allowed and fourth in yards per carry allowed. They've had a stout rush defense all season, especially recently allowing only 221 rushing yards in their past four outings. It could be a tougher assignment, however, if Alex Highsmith (ankle) can't go, as expected. Mike McCarthy said it will be "tough for [Highsmith] to make it this week."

Is there a less impressive team with a great record than the Denver Broncos? Tied for the best mark against the spread entering Week 12 (8-2 ATS), Denver has won six straight games — and could've fairly easily lost four of them. However, its schedule sets up remarkably well for a run at the AFC's No. 1 seed if the Broncos can keep winning as a favorite. Denver is a 3.5-point road favorite in this one at Pittsburgh, and it's hard to find a lot of reasons to be excited about the Steelers going with backup QB Mason Rudolph. And while Bo Nix's Total QBR is only 48.2, Denver's defense is a much better unit than Pittsburgh's. The Steelers' playoff chances continue to dim with a loss here. — Ben Fawkes

Check out more of Ben's work at the Yahoo Sports betting hub.

Scoring expectations are muted (36.5 total) as the Broncos and Steelers meet for a Black Friday afternoon game. Here are three fantasy themes to unpack as you watch the game.

1. Can Mason Rudolph get Pittsburgh's passing game going? Aaron Rodgers has not played well for several weeks, but it was still a shocker when his benching was announced Tuesday night. Rudolph has always been a capable backup through his seven-year career, but his overall stats profile to a less-than-average starter. 3. Is Jaylen Warren still a Circle of Trust guy? Warren was seen as one of fantasy's right answers through the first two months, but he's in a 16-43-0 rushing funk over the last two weeks, with zero touchdowns. Rodgers' slump played into this, but Warren needs a decent start because Rico Dowdle is going to see work, too. — Scott Pianowski
