#2670. Boxing chiefs to assess Fury before Joshua fight following schizophrenia comments

The British Boxing Board of Control will assess Tyson Fury ahead of his hotly anticipated bout against Anthony Joshua following comments he made about hearing voices during a mental health episode.

A new self-titled documentary about the 38-year-old, to be released on Netflix on Friday, goes into detail about his mental health struggles. He and his wife Paris recalled frightening episodes in which he heard voices threatening him and his family after he was hospitalised with a suspected heart attack in 2016.

He said: "Words can't explain the darkness I was in. It was like the living version of the pits of hell's fire. I 100 per cent thought I'd end up in a padded room with the door locked and that scared me so much."

In the original version of the documentary, which has since been edited before release, Paris said he was "mild schizophrenic", although he was not medically diagnosed. Doctors said he had experienced a severe anxiety attack.

Paris clarified her comments to The Mirror on Thursday: "Whilst Tyson did show some symptoms associated with schizophrenia, he doesn't have this condition and has never received a diagnosis. Mental health is complex, and it isn't always easy to find the right words, especially when you're living it with someone you love."

The British Boxing Board of Control said it would evaluate the comments broadcast in the documentary before clearing Fury to box Joshua, with the fight scheduled for 11 December in Cardiff's Principality Stadium.

The board's general secretary, Robert Smith, told BBC Sport: "We are in the process of dealing with the matter but if there are any medical issues we wouldn't let anyone box, doesn't matter if it's Tyson Fury or not, it could be anybody.

"I'm fairly confident he will be absolutely fine. We're dealing with it now and we'll have an answer very shortly.

"If our doctors are satisfied he's fit to box, he will box."

He declined to comment on the specifics of the process, saying, "it's a medical matter".

The board's regulations state that schizophrenia is among psychological conditions which "may preclude" a boxer from obtaining a first licence. An existing licence holder is subject to "such action as in [the board's] absolute discretion it sees fit".

#2669. Questions & Antlers: Early season impressions, featuring Nets Daily’s Anthony Puccio (Part 2)

Last week, we introduced you to Nets Daily's Editor-in-Chief, Anthony Puccio, with the premise that he, as a long-time Brooklyn Nets fan and writer, knows what we're going through this season following our beloved Milwaukee Bucks. In response, you came screaming off a high pick and roll, turned the corner—drawing the strongside defender—and hit him seams up in the corner with your questions. As you'll see below, he didn't let you down with the finish. Nylon.

stoneAge: Did you expect the rebuild to take so long and how far away are the Nets from being a playoff team again?

AP: I expected it to take long, but I figured they would have moved some assets to speed this thing up. I was wrong. We're looking at a Nets team currently two-three years away from playoffs—and that's being generous.

stoneAge: Which of the Nets' current players are part of their future core and what do the Nets lack the most to reach the next level?

AP: Mikel Brown Jr., Egor Dëmin, and Nolan Traore. The Nets lack a lot of things, particularly size in the front court. This isn't new. They lack athleticism. They lack three-point shooters. And they lack basic fundamentals required to build on good habits for a sustainable culture.

Mitchell Maurer: How do you navigate a landscape where so many people in the same geographic area are head-over-heels for the Knicks? A title is (as we've seen around here…) a surefire way to attract bandwagon fans, who are as vocal as they are anonymous 'round these Internet parts. The Nets are not a "nothing" franchise but they clearly don't carry the same weight (broadly speaking) as their cross-town counterparts. It's not a fair paradigm, to be considered an "afterthought" and I'm curious if there's similarities with how Bucks fans may have felt back in the heyday of the Packers and/or Brewers (who also just won a title!)

AP: Nets fans don't want to admit it, but there's absolutely an inferiority. Before the Knicks' chip, the one thing Nets fans had on Knicks fans was a better on-court product since 2000. Now we don't even have that! Put it this way: if you tell someone you're a Nets fan in NY, depending on who you tell, they might say, "Who?" Or "Why?"

Terrapin Revisited: What was it like to adjust expectations when the Nets went from title contenders to "Well, what exactly are we now?" after their big trades? Any recommendations for Bucks fans on how to adapt?

AP: There's no way of sugar-coating it—it feels like a dead end. You adapt when you simply learn to accept this is the new reality, and you never know when it might return. My recommendation: lean on the community to talk. It's difficult without picks to look forward to. Expect the worst, hope the best. Don't turn on each other though. (Editor's note: Sage advice—and one of the things I love about Brew Hoop).

Terrapin Revisited: What have you enjoyed most about the Nets during this rebuilding era? In other words, what can fans focus on as far as the bright side of such teams?

AP: Watching people in the organization make a name for themselves, hustling and shining in the shadows of the down years. Ideally it a player, but it can be any personnel. College basketball, too.

Terrapin Revisited: Do you have any insights on what to expect from veterans on the team at this time? A number of Bucks' vets are disappointing this year, I'm not sure how much that is to be expected when the stakes they are playing for are a lot lower vs. how much that provides some useful insights on the vets. What have you seen from different vets on the Nets?

AP: Right now I see two vets on the Nets who want to get their shots up and head out. It feels like they embrace the leadership role until the losses actually pile up.

Terrapin Revisited: What recommendations can you make on how to watch the development of young players on teams like the Nets and Bucks? What might we watch for—and what might we need to set aside—in order to more effectively watch at present, and appreciate what we have?

AP: It's all a matter of expectations and perspective. Seriously. Watch for where guys say they're working on their games.

Pono: Based on the Nets' rebuilding experience, how should the Bucks navigate developing young players with potential and very young players with potential? For context, last season Ryan Rollins emerged as the Bucks' top young player but this season the full-on rebuild approach has altered his role and, early on, stunted his growth.

AP: This is where the G League needs to become a necessity. Get those very young players burn instead of rotting on bench, trying to force their games. Let them have some time dominating at the lower level, or learning, getting stronger, and ready for when the time comes.

BarryDort: What do you think of the new NBA draft lottery? It seems like it puts more bad teams at the mercy of the ping pong balls. Unless you can somehow get a top five pick, it's really hard to find difference makers as you know from the Nets' last three drafts.

AP: Honestly, it doesn't feel like a long term solution to stop tanking.

Nate O.: With six first-round picks the last two drafts and 11 through 2033, it feels like the Nets are a great example of how to stack assets. I'm curious if you feel like this is a position of strength to be operating from, and only good things can unfold, or are there any other moves you wish the Nets had made or concerns you have moving forward?

AP: Concerns. They have eight players on rookie contracts, and getting them all necessary burn to develop has been extremely difficult. Taking five picks in one round felt a little silly at the time, and it's simply a handful for the coaching staff.

Southern Marxist: The Bucks front office has had to totally shift gears from spending any unused asset in an effort to get Giannis a second championship to accumulating and developing talent. Based on your observations of the Nets front office, what advice would you give the Bucks front office?

AP: Don't wait too long and be as transparent as possible. Fans know things aren't easy right now; I think they'd prefer to know what the direction is instead of paying for a product that's headed nowhere—or looks that way. The Nets keep their fans in the dark related to a lot of things here, and it comes across as disrespectful to paying customers.

I can't tell the experts how to do their job but at least communicate with fans. It's such a dramatic dropoff for the base of the brand—the face of it to—are gone. Reassure people that you can get back and how.

And just like that, our second instalment of Questions & Antlers for the season is in the books. A massive shoutout to Anthony for sharing his wisdom on the Nets and what their rebuilding experience might mean for our Bucks fandom.

For more from Anthony, be sure to check out his work at Nets Daily and follow him on X (@APooch). And for more Questions & Antlers, check back in around the halfway point of the season. Until then, there's plenty of ball to watch—and plenty of coverage to come.

#2664. Leeds United Chase French Striker Rennes Could Sell: Is £39m Worth It?

Leeds United and Everton are reportedly targeting Rennes striker Esteban Lepaul, according to Sport Witness.

The 26-year-old France international scored 20 goals and provided five assists in Ligue 1 last season, then added seven in eight league appearances this term, four of them penalties. Rennes extended his contract to 2030 in June, yet the report says they are preparing for a January or summer exit. Transfermarkt values him at €45m, roughly £39m.

Eliezer Mayenda, a €22m (about £19m) signing, is struggling, so Rennes are already scouting Rosenborg's Amin Chiakha as a replacement in attack.

FotMob's data shows a penalty-box finisher. His 29 shots have produced 16 on target and 5.80 expected goals, and he ranks in the 95th percentile among forwards for goals.

The weaknesses are just as clear. He wins 40.9% of his aerial duels and 37.8% of all duels, and sits in the third percentile for defensive contributions. Only three of his seven goals this season came from open play.

Leeds scored only 10 goals in their first ten league games before beating Chelsea 4-1 last Saturday to reach 17 points from 11. Noah Okafor scored twice there and Dominic Calvert-Lewin, 29, converted a penalty, yet the striker missed 19 big chances in the Premier League last season, according to FotMob.

Farke's back three and two strikers need forwards who press, and Calvert-Lewin has led the Premier League for pressures applied since the start of last season. Lepaul's defensive numbers would test that.

ISTANBUL, TURKEY – AUGUST 2: Anthony Rouault of Rennes interacts with his teammate Esteban Lepaul during the during the pre-season friendly match between Galatasaray SK and Rennes at Rams Park Stadium on August 2, 2026 in Istanbul, Turkey. (Photo by Ahmad Mora/Getty Images)

No, at least not in January and not at £39m or more. Rennes can keep him in Europa League football on a contract until 2030, and TEAMtalk reports Everton lead the chase.

Everton have only Thierno Barry as a senior centre-forward, but Leeds face no such shortage. Their problem is conversion, which makes Lepaul tempting, yet he created just seven chances in 562 minutes and would not help Farke's pressing. Calvert-Lewin started each of Leeds' first ten league games, and Okafor is scoring, so Lepaul would arrive as a rotation option at a starter's price.

A cheaper, pressing-minded forward would suit the back three better. Summer is the sensible window, when Rennes may have Chiakha in place and Calvert-Lewin's age gives succession a stronger case. Paying about £39m for 20 goals is fair only if the player can also defend from the front, and Lepaul's numbers say he cannot yet.

In the least surprising development in the NBA on Wednesday, the Knicks beat the Cavaliers.

Here are very few quotes from yesterday's affair and elsewhere. Enjoy Thanksgiving today, and make sure to save the leftovers!

On the benefits of potentially missing the NBA Cup knockout rounds:

"It is important (to win and potentially advance), but the reality of it is, when you look at the schedule, and you see that our percentage [to advance] is not that high, and so they kind of shared with me what our schedule would look like if we don't go and if we do go. And you look at it, you're like, 'Whoa, that's a lot of days off if you don't go.' And so again, you want to compete; you want to win. But if you don't, in my opinion, when you look at the schedule… you're like, there's an opportunity if you got some guys banged up to get rest and/or to work on some things in between the games that you have if you're not involved in the Cup."

On the physical and mental toll of competing in the NBA Cup:

"I didn't really break it down to an 83rd game, but when I talk about the Cup, it adds a level of stress maybe on your mind and your body because the games are intense as you go along and you're playing more games in a short amount of time.

"I remember it was like, game, game, game, and then you win the Cup, and you celebrate it that night, and you hop on a plane and go play in Indiana the next night. And so it's great. You like the competition and the setup, but it adds a lot of stress to you physically and mentally. I'm saying this because especially with the extended season we had last year and how taxing the games were for our playoff run mentally and physically, I'm trying to be smart, so if — knock on wood — we end up advancing, I'll try to be smart about it."

Then they lost in the second year, but they set a regular season record of 73 wins, and one of the things that he used to tell me, they gassed themselves trying to get this record and come playoff time they just didn't have enough in the tank to close it. #2659. NFL picks: Who the experts predict to win in the Broncos-Steelers game

The Denver Broncos (8-2) will be looking for their first victory in Pittsburgh since 2006 when they take on the Steelers (6-4) on Black Friday. They will also look to stay ahead of the Kansas City Chiefs, who play on Thanksgiving, in the race for first place in the AFC West.

The Broncos have not lost since Week 4, winning each of their last six games to put them on the same kind of pace they were on last year at this time, when they ended up with the No. 1 seed in the AFC. Defeating a Steelers team starting its backup quarterback following a disastrous week seems like a must for Denver.

How do the experts see this one shaking out? Let's take a look.

"This Friday game pits two teams who would be in the playoffs right now," wrote Prisco for CBS. "But the Steelers have lost two straight and haven't looked good. Denver has won six in a row. But I think the Steelers will find a way to show up and win this one behind their running game. It won't be pretty, but the Steelers will find a way."

"The Steelers are in a tough spot here after back-to-back losses in the AFC North race," wrote Bender for The Sporting News. "Aaron Rodgers averages 180 passing yards the last two weeks, and he's taken eight sacks. Jonah Coleman is coming off a 113-yard, three-TD performance for the Broncos. Pittsburgh is 4-0 S/U at home this season, and the Steelers deliver at home."

EDIT: This prediction was made before the Steelers benched and then released Aaron Rodgers.

"The Broncos are starting to put it together on offense, while the Steelers' offense is falling apart," wrote Cluff for Arizona Republic. "Jonah Coleman and Denver will extend their win streak to seven games with a big win on the road, handing Pittsburgh a third straight loss and its first loss at home this season."

"Forget rolling back prices -- roll back your expectations for Pittsburgh on Black Friday. It would be bad enough if the Steelers were only dealing with a miserable slump over the past two weeks, during which they've been outscored 37-6 in the first half of consecutive losses. But Pittsburgh also must prepare to face an 8-2 Broncos squad amid a soap operatic couple of days that included the benching of Aaron Rodgers late Tuesday night; Rodgers going on The Pat McAfee Show on Wednesday to give his version of events before declaring he would not be returning to the team; and ultimately, the Steelers' release of the 42-year old quarterback. Those events have created a uniquely disruptive environment while Pittsburgh prepares to play Denver on a short week. Mason Rudolph will now serve as the Steelers' starter, but he's a known entity at this point of his career. The 31-year-old has a 9-9-1 record with 4,927 passing yards, 30 touchdowns and 22 interceptions. He has not been the type to elevate players to a degree necessary to take down a Super Bowl contender. The Broncos seemingly have multiple routes to a victory: They could certainly end up blowing out a team dealing with turmoil, but even if the Steelers rise to the occasion, Pittsburgh lacks the offensive punch to pull away from Denver. Should it end up close late, the Broncos are very comfortable with that script. Through 10 games this season, Bo Nix already has a league-leading five fourth-quarter comebacks and six game-winning drives."

The rest of the panel at NFL.com, Brooke Cersosimo, Gennaro Filice, Dan Parr and Jeremy Bergman all chose the Broncos as well.

#2658. The stealing, running Mavs are the perfect cast for a high-IQ duo that could change basketball

The Mavericks just beat a very good Denver Nuggets team through aggressive defense, forcing steals, and running on offense. It is indeed a new day in Dallas.

Kyrie Irving, a player that has pretty much seen it all by now, didn't even have an efficient night (5/19 on field goal attempts, 1/8 from three). He did, however, lead the team to a victory that shows the whole league that the Dallas Mavericks now are the exact opposite of who they used to be.

In a gesture as moving as it was telling, Kyrie showed the world that he and Cooper Flagg have the rarest of connections. This is a high-IQ duo who could change the trajectory of what basketball looks like. And they may be on the way to doing that as we speak.

It is not only the gesture that's important here, it's the ultimate look away pass and the back door cut by Flagg that shows a connection between the two, usually built through years of ups and downs. It was almost like they could read each other's minds. This is what real chemistry looks like.

Kirk Henderson said it best: "There are lookaway passes, then there's something like this where I feel as if Kyrie's head never even moved the direction where Coop cut to."

Jamal Crawford interpreted the gesture as "me and you", and either way this is a gesture of connection, we – as in us – we got this. And even though Kyrie meant Cooper, we all feel it a little bit.

You may be watching from across the globe, you may not even be a Mavs fan, but anybody watching, knowing what this team and city have gone through recently, felt it.

Because no one has worked harder to get the Dallas Mavericks back together than Kyrie Irving. After it was torn apart, he did everything he could to hold it together. He mentored, he was everyone's vet, he led, he coached when injured – he showed the way and the light in the dark times.

And Dallas is reaping the benefits right now. That is also why it felt so touching, seeing the vet who worked so hard to hold it all together, make this gesture to the young superstar with the highest ceiling imaginable.

They took away his running mate, his brother and a genuine friendship and on-court chemistry, resulting in the most negative period in Dallas, in which he forced himself to play too much and carry more than he should have. His resulting ACL injury took him away from his craft for more than a year, and now – finally – his hard work is really paying off. Kyrie Irving deserves this.

And despite the spiritual experience it can be to watch Irving play, especially when he has chemistry with his teammates, he didn't carry the team to this extraordinary win. Neither did his co-star Flagg really.

It was a cast of teammates who decided to outwork, outhustle and believe in their connection, along with a well-prepared coach, who had clearly done a lot of work to get this team ready. It was no easy feat. But the Mavs made it look easy.

They had 13 steals. The league leader averages 10.6 (Los Angeles Lakers). The Mavs average 9.44 this season, but led by the surprising hero of the last games, Caleb Martin, with five, they kept the pressure on the passing lanes all game, stressing the Nuggets in a way we don't see every day. Not only that, they had 16 steals last game versus Utah, and a whopping 50 steals the last four games (which all happen to be wins).

Martin started this game on fire on both ends, secured the first six points by knocking down two threes in a row and continued to force five steals in the first half, constantly the first to run in transition.

This is exactly the leadership a team needs from a role player next to superstars, and with Zaccharie Risacher next to him, the two have the potential to cause havoc defensively on every team in the league, followed by easy transition points, if they keep this up.

Caleb Martin explained the game plan in the half:

"High sense of urgency. A high level of respect for a great team," he said during the broadcast.

He went on to explain that steals were an emphasis, as well as just being active. "The more active we are," Martin said, "sense of urgency, the better a team we are, positive things happen".

And not even interview questions were about to distract Caleb Martin, who is on a mission in Dallas right now.

When asked in the half whether the loud colors of the court, which are usually a little on the bright side during Cup games, was giving him a headache, too, he answered deadpan:

"I don't know, I'm trying to win a game right now."

#2653. How Moe Wagner and Danny Wolf have become offensive bright spots for the Nets

It's pretty doom and gloom in NetsWorld right now, and that's justified. Sitting at 3-13 after Monday night's blowout against the Minnesota Timberwolves, the team has now suffered nine double-digit losses this season.

When a young, rebuilding team isn't winning, it's one thing, but getting completely outmatched consistently is another. That's pretty much what's been the case for Brooklyn, as nine of their 13 losses have come by 10+ points.

Interestingly, one of the biggest questions entering the season surrounded Brooklyn's frontcourt. It wasn't clear how the rotation would take shape.

Day'Ron Sharpe entered the season as the team's starting center following Nic Claxton's departure, while Moe Wagner arrived in free agency. Wagner's health was in question after he played just 66 games over the previous two seasons, including time missed due to a torn ACL. Danny Wolf was another question mark after an up-and-down rookie campaign.

So far, the frontcourt has produced more offense than expected. Brooklyn's rim protection remains a work in progress, and its defense has struggled at every level. But offensively, two of the team's biggest surprises have been Wagner and Wolf.

Offensively, two of Brooklyn's biggest surprises have been Wagner and Wolf.

Wagner has been known for his offensive game since entering the league—most notably his success from beyond the arc and his consistency.

Although injuries have hindered him significantly over the past two years, Wagner is starting to pick up where he left off before the ACL injury forced him out of action for 98 games.

Through 16 games, Wagner owns a 70.7% effective field-goal percentage, ranking in the 98th percentile among bigs, per Cleaning the Glass. A large part of that production comes from his remarkable 62.5% shooting from three-point range. That percentage almost certainly won't hold over an 82-game season, but it's an encouraging start to his Brooklyn tenure.

What's even more encouraging, though, is the success beyond just the 3-point line. For a big like Wagner, who isn't necessarily touted for rim protection or stout defense, being a multi-faceted offensive contributor is crucial.

Overall, he's returning to the offense that worked at the peak of his career in Orlando. Last season with the Magic, just 44% of his overall attempts came at the rim, while 25% came from the midrange. This year, those numbers have shifted to 60% and 19%, respectively. That's much more in line with what we saw from Wagner during his two most efficient seasons (2023-24, 2024-25), with his effective FG percentage finishing north of 60% in both of those campaigns.

Wagner has also improved drastically at creating his own shot. Last season, 88% of his made baskets at the rim were assisted. Meanwhile, that has dropped to 61%, despite a 15-percentage-point increase in his shot usage around the basket.

Obviously, there's only so much that Wagner could be expected to do. Signed to a two-year, $18.4 million contract this offseason, he was widely viewed as the Nets' backup big behind Sharpe. So far, that has held. Sharpe has started all 17 of Brooklyn's games, while averaging 24 minutes per game. Meanwhile, off the bench, Wagner has averaged 17.1 minutes a game.

Entering the season, one of the biggest concerns with the Nets' roster was where points would come from off the bench. So far, their bench scoring hasn't been too shabby, ranking 13th in bench points per game (38.7). More impressively, though, their bench ranks 11th in 3-point percentage (35.7%). Wagner is clearly a big reason behind that.

Having a big who can stretch the floor while also generating offense around the basket is a luxury.

The bigger question mark entering the year is what the Nets really had in Wolf. Just like the four Flatbush 5 members behind Egor Dëmin, whose start to the year had been disappointing, the Michigan product had a lot to prove heading into the season.

So far, though, that development has been encouraging. Just like Wagner, the 27th overall pick in last June's draft has emerged as a threat from beyond the arc. After shooting just 32% from deep as a rookie, he is converting at 46.7% this season, ranking in the 95th percentile among bigs.

Worth noting, though, he only played four minutes in Wednesday's win over the Milwaukee Bucks after exiting with left knee soreness.

There has also been an uptick in volume: 54% of his overall shot attempts have come from the 3-point range, up from 44% a season ago. His mark this year ranks in the 88th percentile among bigs. Beyond that, 35% of his overall attempts have come from non-corner 3s, which ranks in the 91st percentile.

Wolf's output has also had a large impact on Brooklyn as a whole. Last season, the Nets scored 5.1 fewer points per 100 possessions with him on the floor than with him on the bench. This season, they're scoring 5.4 more points per 100 possessions with him out there, ranking in the 83rd percentile among all players.

Additionally, the Nets' effective field-goal percentage improves by 3.2 percentage points with him on the floor, while the offensive rebounding percentage also rises by 8.3 percentage points. The latter ranks in the 96th percentile among players who have logged a minute this season. For context, he has only played 244 minutes this season, but those numbers are still fascinating.

Even more interesting is how he's been used. After opening the season outside of Jordi Fernández's rotation, Wolf has worked his way into the lineup, but in an odd spot: as the Nets' starting shooting guard. How many people had that on their bingo card entering the season?

In fact, six of his seven starts this season have come at the 2.

Against the Magic on Friday night, Fernández inserted Wolf into the starting five for Dëmin, and Wolf responded with a 20-point outing. In his second straight start, against the Minnesota Timberwolves on Monday, he finished with 11 points, four assists, and five rebounds on 4-of-7 shooting, including 3-of-5 from deep.

As our own Anthony Puccio noted earlier this month, Wolf played every second of his initial breakout performance against the Charlotte Hornets alongside either Sharpe or Wagner. That trend has held mostly true since then, letting him work away from the basket and avoid many traditional big responsibilities.

Is he truly a 5 in the NBA? There need to be more reps to make the case for or against it, but he doesn't ideally fit as a shooting guard. At 6'11", it's just not a natural fit, and it is easy for him to get exposed guarding shifty playmaking guards at the top of the key. Even though he was a ball handler at Michigan, being a guard in college versus the NBA are two completely different responsibilities. Nonetheless, the versatility is highly encouraging.

Regardless of where Wolf ultimately settles in the long term, he and Wagner have given the Nets more offensively than anyone could have asked for before the season.

#2651. Lions score touchdown after Dan Campbell opts for safety on Bears' illegal batting penalty

The high-powered Thanksgiving matchup between the Detroit Lions and the Chicago Bears delivered early, with a wild sequence just before halftime. After accepting a potentially risky safety on an unusual Bears penalty, the Lions converted a touchdown to close out the first half with a 19-10 lead.

The potentially game-changing sequence started after the two-minute warning in the second quarter, with Chicago quarterback Caleb Williams getting sacked and fumbling the ball at the Bears' two-yard line.

Once out of Williams' hands, the ball bounced past multiple players into the Chicago end zone. Bears offensive lineman Darnell Wright, in an effort to stave off a safety, used a close fist to bat the ball out of the end zone, where Lions defensive back Brian Branch was able to get his hands on it.

But Wright's efforts to get the ball out of the end zone were not allowed: The lineman was flagged for "illegal batting," which results in a safety if the call is accepted.

The situation presented Lions head coach Dan Campbell with a decision: Take the safety and try to put together a touchdown drive before halftime, or decline the penalty to get the ball and set up a red-zone drive.

Campbell decided to go for the safety, giving him and the Lions a minute and change to grab a touchdown and justify the choice.

Initially, the drive got off to a concerning start: The Lions, who had already been called for two false starts earlier in the quarter, picked up two more false start penalties in a row to set up third-and-12. Jared Goff then erased some of the distance by finding Jahmyr Gibbs for an 11-yard reception, but the catch fell just short of first down.

On fourth-and-1, though, Detroit pulled off a gutsy and successful quarterback sneak, giving Goff the two-yard rush to keep the drive going. That set up a massive 39-yard throw from Goff to Jameson Williams, before another first down to Gibbs, and a successful touchdown throw to Sam LaPorta.

In an interview on the broadcast after halftime, Campbell told CBS that the number of timeouts left — the Bears had two at the time, while the Lions had all three — and his faith in his players led him to go for the full nine-point play. He praised Jameson Williams and Goff for their plays, and said that he "just felt good" about the offense's chances to find the end zone.

Illegal batting, the penalty that sparked the whole sequence, is a relative rarity in the league. One of the only recent examples came against the Lions, with Seattle Seahawks linebacker K.J. Wright batting a fumble out of the end zone in 2015, though the foul was not flagged. The NFL later admitted that the penalty should have been called.

#2639. Maryland men’s basketball blows late lead in 75-71 loss to San Diego State

With five minutes remaining in its game against San Diego State, it appeared Mike McNair Jr. and Maryland men's basketball had engineered a storybook comeback in the Players Era Tournament.

Playing basketball on the West Coast for the first time in over two years, the California native scored 16 points as part of a 19-7 Maryland run that turned the game on its head. But the Terps made just two baskets over the final 4:50 of the game, with one coming as time expired.

For the second time in three days, Maryland came up short in a gritty game, as a 16-3 San Diego State run sealed a 75-71 loss for the Terps.

With the defeat, they fell to 0-4 against teams with a winning record.

Every point scored by McNair and the rest of Maryland's guard group was critical. San Diego State completely neutralized the Terps' frontcourt, holding Pharrel Payne and Tomislav Buljan to one combined field goal and nine combined points.

The defensive efforts were led by Jeremiah "Bear" Cherry, who finished with nine blocks, a San Diego State record, alongside 10 points, six rebounds and three steals.

After struggling mightily from 3-point range against Tennessee in their first game, the Terps began Thursday with a concerted effort attacking the paint. But San Diego State was ready, logging three blocks in the opening three minutes as Maryland started 0-for-10 from the floor.

The Aztecs couldn't create a sizable early lead, though. The Terps succeeded defensively as much as they struggled offensively, smothering the Aztecs and denying them second chances.

Seven minutes and 55 seconds into the game, Andre Mills scored the Terps' first basket, a transition layup immediately after San Diego State's sixth turnover of the game.

With Buljan benched after picking up two quick fouls and Payne being marked out of the game, DJ Wagner drove Maryland's offense, scoring or assisting five of Maryland's first six baskets.

The point guard also broke a team streak of 20 consecutive misses beyond the arc halfway through the first frame after leaping to corral a ball and turning it into a quick 3-point attempt.

While the Terps' characteristic 3-point struggles continued, their rebounding struggles were new. The Aztecs dominated the glass, particularly in the absence of Buljan.

Before the Croatian took the bench with his second foul, the Terps outrebounded the Aztecs 9-8. For the rest of the frame, San Diego State outrebounded Maryland 13-5, pushing the lead as high as 10 points.

But suddenly, with five minutes remaining in the first half, the Terps flipped a switch. Four consecutive 3-pointers fell for Maryland, each scored by a different player.

That cut the San Diego State lead to three points. However, Maryland couldn't come closer than that on either side of the half.

Finally, 6:23 into the second half, the Terps earned their first lead. McNair drained a pair of catch-and-shoot 3-pointers, and Kaden House earned and converted two free throws to cap an 8-0 run — Maryland's longest run of the game. McNair finished with a season-high 22 points and six made 3-pointers.

The Terps grew their lead to as many as seven points. But the Aztecs refused to roll over, earning back the lead with 3:10 remaining.

The third lead change of the night was the deciding one, with San Diego State ending the game 7-of-7 from the free throw line to drop Maryland to 3-4 on the season.

1. McNair homecoming. When the Terps took on San Diego State — whose campus McNair grew up an hour away from — the California native had his father and fiancée sitting in the front row.

Midway through the second half, McNair exploded onto the scene, scoring 16 of 19 points as Maryland turned the game around. When he subbed off the court with eight minutes remaining, his family, coaches and teammates all lined up in a row for high-fives and celebrations — celebrations that were short-lived for the Terps.

2. A balanced offensive effort undoes Maryland. Only six San Diego State players scored in the game, but all six of them got into double digits. The Terps were stout defensively early on, but they allowed the Aztecs to shoot 50% from the floor in the second half.

3. Better showing from Baba Oladotun. While the freshman hasn't immediately lived up to his sky-high expectations, Oladotun was an important part of Maryland's rotation Thursday. He had four points on 2-of-6 shooting and also added three assists, two rebounds and a block. He clearly earned the trust of Williams, playing 24 minutes — the most of his career by a significant margin.

#2636. What we learned from the Spurs’ loss to the Trail Blazers

One of the few things I hope for as a spectator is that teams playing the late-night game bring it. It's too hard to stay awake as it is after a long day, so fans need excitement to keep them from falling asleep. Fortunately, it was not a problem for these teams, yet the only issue the San Antonio Spurs had late was their basketball IQ.

I had this game circled on the calendar because the physicality was off the charts the last time they played on Nov. 7. It appears it was not a distant memory for the Portland Trail Blazers, as the ESPN broadcast highlighted how they felt embarrassed by that game and wanted their lick back. Nonetheless, it was grown-up hoops and it wouldn't be a surprise if these squads didn't like each other.

Wednesday night being an Emirates Cup game added to the fun because the winner would keep their hopes alive of getting to the quarterfinal, still needing to get by Friday's game. Keep in mind that getting to the next round guarantees the players $60,499 and half of that for the two-way guys.

I wish that coach Mitch Johnson hadn't stuck to his usual substitution patterns in the third quarter, because when Wembanyama sat the Spurs were instantly outscored by eight. They got back on track when Victor checked in to clean up the mess, and the team likely could have separated itself had he had a longer shift. Games like this with absences to key guys magnify every decision. While the most part Mitch was good, I shook my head as he tried to buy time for the starters with Carter Bryant and Ja'Kobi Gillespie at the start of the fourth.

Johnson was probably thinking about preserving his main guys for later games, but this wasn't this a big one? Every now and then, 40 minutes against good teams is not so bad, and he probably would have broken 50 points for the third time this year.

Aside from their cup chances, the three late turnovers and failure to stop Portland's two 3-pointers ruined Wemby's 44-point masterpiece. Of course, the Trail Blazers deserve credit, but the Spurs also beat themselves down the stretch. Stephon Castle's eight-second violation was a killer.

Props to coach Micah Nori. He has a serious team, while he's basically on a prove-it deal, and they've been without Ja Morant. A lot of it has to do with them having one of the most balanced teams in the league, and it helps that Damian Lillard is still one sport'a clutch shooters. He has come back from his Achilles tear with his first step intact, and his outburst in the second half was vintage.

Without De'Aaron Fox and Dylan Harper, the Spurs were without two of the league's best penetrators (sorely needed against a high-level defense) which is a big reason why Wemby was the only one to score more than six points in the lane. The Spurs only had two quarters in which the offense was running smoothly (posting a 112.1 offensive rating) and that is one of their four-worst showings of the season. Portland was able to slow them down by making them pass less often.

Wembanyama stepped up. He poured in jumpers as Portland got physical with him. He kept the pressure on Donovan Clingan and fouled him out with four minutes left. In the past, Wembanyama wouldn't always assert himself in those situations and now it's like radar is beeping when his man gets five personals.

The Spurs mostly get the shot they are looking for when running the horns set, which has a screen to the left and right for the ball handler. The team has the best results on these when the screener is the scorer and the ball handler is the decoy.

Bryant should model his game after Keldon Johnson's. The latter barely scored but has mastered the art of hustle and had 12 rebounds, including five offensive, on Wednesday.

Portland is arguably the best paint-attacking team in the league, averaging 61.7 drives per game, and Deni Avdija has a lot to do with that.

Wembanyama had 12 points in the third quarter when he was subbed out and had only logged 21 total minutes to that point. As his rampage was paused, I was reminded of the old joke about how the only person who could stop Michael Jordan was Dean Smith.

#2630. The Lakers will need help to advance in the NBA Cup

In news that should shock no one, the Kings sit at the bottom of Group C in the NBA Cup this year, winless in four games.

Above them sit four teams, including the Lakers, at 2-1. Each has a path to advance as we head into Friday, the final day of NBA Cup play, setting up an exciting finish.

The Spurs and Lakers will have their anticipated showdown on Friday evening. At the same time, the Warriors and Blazers square off in Portland. All four teams need a win and results going their way in the other game to advance, setting up some good ol' scoreboard watching during the game.

So, let's look at how the Lakers can win the group and their much slimmer path to a wild card spot.

The Lakers' desire to beat the Spurs on Friday likely centers on making a statement against arguably the top team in the Western Conference. The added bonus, perhaps, is that they can advance in the NBA Cup as well.

Any path out of the group requires a win on Friday. A loss drops them to 2-2 in the group and with two teams guaranteed to finish with just one loss, the Lakers can't advance as a wild card with a loss.

But winning isn't enough. The Lakers' loss to the Warriors in Golden State — a game they led by 25 points — leaves them needing help to move on. If LA and Portland both win, the Lakers hold the head-to-head tiebreaker and win the group. However, if Golden State upsets the Blazers in Portland, then that Halloween Eve loss stings a bit more as the Warriors will top the group.

Those two-leg scenarios exist for each side. Portland must win and have the Spurs win to win the group while San Antonio needs a victory and a Warriors upset to do the same.

However, winning the group isn't the only way to advance to the knockout rounds.

Along with the three group winners, one wild card advances to the knockout rounds. For the Lakers, this only comes into play if they win and the Warriors win, leaving them with just one loss in the group.

Point differential is how the wild card spot is determined and the Lakers aren't in an ideal spot. LA's close win one week ago over the Kings didn't offset the big loss to the Warriors. As a result, they enter the final game with a -9 point differential.

The simplest way for all this to play out is for the Wolves, who may be without LaMelo Ball, to beat the Grizzlies, leaving no one-loss teams in Group B. Then the tiebreaker will be between the Lakers and the Nuggets.

Denver has a -3 point differential, but get to play the Jazz, who are winless in the NBA Cup. If both the Nuggets and Lakers win, LA would have to beat Denver's margin of victory by at least seven points, assuming Denver wins.

The potential wrench in these plans is the Grizzlies-Wolves contest. Coming into Friday, Minnesota has a +39 point differential and Memphis is at +18. If the Grizzlies win a close game, then the Wolves likely have the inside track at the wild card spot. It would take a really big Memphis win to bring the Wolves into the point differential range of the Lakers and Nuggets.

These wild card races always have so many moving parts, so here's perhaps the simplest rooting guide for Friday:

Grizzlies huge blowout win or loss at Wolves

#2628. Millville survives storm, stuffs Vineland on Thanksgiving

VINELAND – The 155th edition of the Millville-Vineland high school football game will be remembered for a long time around these neighboring towns.

While the scoreboard confirmed the Thunderbolts won the game, 17-0, the true victor on this Thanksgiving Day was Mother Nature.

While a steady rainfall along with gusty winds whipping around Gittone Stadium made the football tough to hold onto, it couldn't loosen Millville's grip on the victory trophy.

More: Everything you need to know for the 2026 high school football season

The Thunderbolts won for the seventh time in a row, increasing their lead to 69-67-19 in the all-time series, which began in 1893. Over the seven-year successful stretch, Millville has outscored Vineland, 296-33.

Most of the players were headed to the school buses as the clock hit zeroes, not even waiting around for the chance to touch the Tony Surace/John Pierantozzi Victory Cup.

"It was crazy," Millville senior quarterback Robbie O'Connor said about the elements, which would have challenged even the most dedicated mailman on this day.

"When you see all the other games get moved (because of the forecasted storm), maybe this game should have been moved, too. But we love football, and every single game we've played in the rain this year, we've played amazing. We just go out there and do our thing."

Despite the rough conditions, Millville handled its job without a hitch.

The Thunderbolts' special teams produced a safety (off a Vineland botched snap on a punt in the end zone) and a Jack Powers 27-yard field goal. The defense delivered five takeaways, including a scoop-and-score by Nyshon Jones while the offense accounted for the other TD with Jachere Graves's 1-yard TD run.

While there were a couple hundred die-hard fans in the stands on both sides of the stadium, the weather kept many in the warmth of their own homes.

And that's what Millville head coach Humberto Ayala was upset about the most.

"It was ridiculous (to play)," Ayala said. "This is a historic game, it's the seniors' last game. And in my personal opinion, it's not fair to those seniors and those kids, not to have the fans here for them on this last game of the season.

"This game means so much, it's the 155th time we've played them, and they should have put a better thought process into it, instead of worrying about a potential advantage for them.

"Honestly, we should have played (Wednesday night) or they should have moved it to another day. In the end, the result was the result and we knew what we were going to do."

In a rivalry that has always produced plenty of heat (even on this day), this was another undoubtably another log on the fire.

And that's OK with Vineland head coach Dan Russo.

"I'm happy we played," he said. "Last time I checked, it's football, not golf.

"This game is played on Thanksgiving and we're trying to keep this tradition alive. If we played on grass or if we were located down the shore, we would have moved the game to another day. I thought it was in our best interest to play on Thanksgiving."

Russo didn't deny that playing in the rainy and windy conditions suited the Fighting Clan better than the Millville offense, which is more pass-heavy. But he also pointed out that Vineland encountered a lot more problems holding onto the football than Millville.

"It certainly hurt us more than them (Thursday)," Russo said.

Reporters' notes from the game were no match for the elements either, but they weren't the only object to suffer a loss. The Surace/Pierantozzi Victory Cup was missing its large base, which had broken off earlier in the morning en route to Gittone Stadium.

Unofficial stats had O'Connor completing five passes for 35 yards. The weather kept the senior quarterback from making a serious run at two passing records. For one of those marks, he needed 285 yards to become just the second quarterback in South Jersey history to throw for 2,000 in three different seasons, joining Timber Creek's Devin Leary.

While he would have liked a better opportunity to go after the records, O'Connor put the game in perspective.

"This is one of the biggest rivalries in the entire country," he said. "It means a lot to our city, so it means a lot to us.

"It's a privilege to wear the orange and blue and I'm so happy I got the opportunity to do so these last three years."

The elements certainly made it tough to grabe the football, so imagine what it took to kick in Thursday's conditions.

After a bad snap thwarted his first field goal attempt earlier in the game, Powers gave Millville an 11-0 lead just before halftime with a 27-yards field goal.

The sophomore converted 6-of-11 field goal attempts and 28 of 31 extra points this season. Two of his field goals were from beyond 40 yards.

Millville finished at 7-5 for the second consecutive season and locked up its fifth winning campaign since Ayala took over the program. The Thunderbolts lost to Atlantic City, 35-14, in the Central Jersey Group 4 championship on Nov. 13.

Vineland went 5-5 in Russo's return to the program. Russo went 42-60, including the program's first-ever playoff wins, during his first stretch as the Fighting Clan's head coach.

"We're taking the right steps, we're moving forward," Russo said. "This was a fun group to coach and we're hungry to fix it. Now, we're going to get them prepared for next year."

Vineland lost to Sayreville, 29-27, in the Central Jersey Group 5 quarterfinal round.

#2624. Ranking The Best 3-Level Scorers In The NBA Right Now

Being one of the best scorers in the NBA doesn't necessarily mean you're one of the best three-level scorers. Just look at Giannis Antetokounmpo, who's been putting up 30 PPG for years without needing much of a three-point shot, or Stephen Curry, who can go for 40 points without even touching the paint (though I'd say he's definitely inside this category).

When we talk about three-level scoring, we're looking at guys who can get their points in three different areas of the court. The first one is inside the paint, whether that's through post-ups, layups, dunks, or floaters. The second is the mid-range, where we get most of those pull-up jumpers and fadeaways, and the third is obviously scoring from beyond the arc.

What makes these guys so difficult to guard is that taking away one shot doesn't take them out of the game. Go under a screen, and they'll pull up from three. Play too high, and they'll get to the rim. Drop your big man too far into the paint, and they'll get an open jumper from the elbow.

For this ranking, we're looking at scoring production from each area, shooting efficiency, volume, and how good these players are at creating their own shots. We're also putting more weight on what they've been doing this season rather than their glory or reputation, with all stats coming from the 2026-27 regular season.

With that in mind, here are the 10 best three-level scorers in the NBA right now.

It feels a little weird having Kevin Durant this low on a list like this, considering he's probably one of the five best three-level scorers we've ever seen. But at 38 years old, the Houston Rockets forward is taking just 13.5 shots per game, his lowest volume since coming into the NBA.

The efficiency is still there, though. Durant is shooting 50.8% from the field, 39.7% from three, and 88.1% from the free-throw line, good for a 64.9% true shooting mark. He's also making 55.6% of his two-point attempts, so it's not like he's suddenly having problems scoring inside the arc.

Durant ranks sixth in the NBA in mid-range scoring at 4.5 points per game, which accounts for around 21% of his entire scoring production. He's still getting to those same spots around the elbows, shooting over smaller defenders in the post, and pulling up from pretty much anywhere inside the three-point line.

The biggest change is how often he's getting those shots. Durant is attempting only 4.1 threes per game and scoring six points in the paint, with another 6.2 points coming from free throws. He's getting fewer opportunities to attack the rim and letting guys like Alperen Sengun and Amen Thompson handle more of the scoring this year.

In terms of pure scoring ability, I'd still take Durant over a good number of players on this list. But there are younger guys producing a lot more across all three levels this season.

For someone who's only 6-foot-3, Donovan Mitchell gets an absurd amount of his scoring done inside the paint. The Cleveland Cavaliers guard is at 10.9 points from that area, which puts him right alongside Shai Gilgeous-Alexander and ahead of plenty of starting centers around the league.

Mitchell is shooting 59.8% on two-point attempts this season, and a lot of that comes from how explosive he is getting downhill. He's strong finishing through contact, can get above the rim when there's a chance, and has a good floater when the opposing big man steps up to contest the drive.

Then there's his three-point shot, which is still a huge part of his game even though he's shooting just 34.4% from deep this season. Mitchell has made 45 threes through 18 games and is taking 7.3 attempts per night, most of the time being able to get into his shot straight off the dribble (40% unassisted 3P).

The reason I've got him ninth is his mid-range production. He's 27th in the NBA with 2.1 points per game from that area, and while we know he can knock down those pull-up jumpers coming off screens, we don't see him go to them anywhere near as much as some of the guys coming up.

Still, averaging 25.0 points on 49.5% shooting from the field while getting almost 44% of your scoring inside the paint as a 6-foot-3 guard is impressive. Mitchell is just more dangerous at two of the three levels than he is at the other one.

There are very few long wings who have such a versatile scoring game as Jayson Tatum. The Boston Celtics star can back down smaller guards, drive past bigger forwards, hit turnaround jumpers from the post, and create his own three-point shot without needing a screen.

He's putting up 27.3 points per game, fifth in the NBA, while taking 20.1 shots and 8.6 threes per game. Interestingly enough, his scoring production from inside the paint and beyond the arc is almost identical, with both areas giving him around 8.8 points per night.

Tatum has already made 47 threes in 16 games, although his 34.3% shooting from deep isn't anything special. He's also shooting exactly 50.0% on two-point attempts, and his overall 43.3% shooting from the field and 57.6% true shooting are a big part of why he's not higher here.

My thing with Tatum is that I'd love to see him go back to his mid-range a little more often. He's giving the Celtics just 2.9 points per game from there, and considering his size and ability to shoot over defenders, he doesn't always need to settle for a difficult stepback three.

The ability is clearly there, and getting to the line 8.3 times per game (7.0 FTM) also helps him maintain his scoring numbers when those jumpers aren't falling. But there are guys averaging fewer points than Tatum who are currently doing a better job of balancing their shot selection and efficiency across all three levels.

When somebody asks me what a three-level scorer looks like, Devin Booker is usually one of the first players I think of. There isn't one specific shot that makes up most of his scoring, and he's one of the few guards who still spends a good portion of every game working from the mid-post.

Booker ranks third in the NBA in mid-range scoring this season, behind SGA and Scottie Barnes, who is developing amazingly in that area if you've seen a few Raptors highlights. Back to the point, around 22% of Booker's points come from that area, which is a much higher percentage than most of the other guards averaging over 20 points in today's NBA.

Watching him come off a screen and get to either elbow is probably the best example of how he uses all three levels. He can reject the screen and get to the rim, stop for a pull-up jumper against a drop, or step back behind the arc if the defender goes under the screen. He's also got the footwork to turn those mismatches into post-ups and fadeaways against smaller guards.

The three-point efficiency hasn't been great this season, with the Phoenix Suns star shooting 32.7% on 5.8 attempts per game. That's a big reason why his overall field goal percentage is down to 46.2%, and he's currently at around 59.0% in true shooting.

What's interesting is that Booker is still making 92.1% of his free throws and getting roughly 6.2 points per game at the line, so the touch is obviously there. If he gets his three-point percentage back into the high 30s, I could easily see him moving into the top five of this ranking.

If we were ranking the best post scorers in the NBA, Nikola Jokic would probably be my first pick. The Denver Nuggets MVP has pretty much every move you could ask for down low, and he doesn't need to be particularly fast or jump particularly high to get his shot off, even with his early-season struggles.

Jokic is sixth in the NBA with 13.9 points per game in the paint, meaning more than half of his entire scoring production comes from inside. He's shooting 60.0% on two-point attempts and 53.0% from the field overall, with just 17.9 shots per game.

The craziest part about his interior scoring is how many different ways he gets those points. There are the little hook shots with either hand, floaters from six or seven feet, spin moves against bigger centers, and those quick volleyball-type shots he gets off before the help defense has time to arrive.

Move him a few feet away from the basket, and he's still got his one-legged fadeaway, turnaround jumpers, and that Sombor Shuffle we all know by now. Jokic doesn't take a ton of mid-range shots, but it's one of the toughest parts of his game to defend because of how high he releases the ball.

What's keeping him outside the top five is his current three-point percentage. Jokic is just 20-of-67 from deep through 16 games, good for 29.9%, after shooting 38.0% last season. He's still at 61.3% in true shooting, but his three-point production isn't close to what some of the players ahead of him are giving their teams right now.

I don't think people realized how much better Victor Wembanyama has gotten as a pure scorer this season. As fun as it was watching a 7-foot-4 big man pull up from 30 feet during his first few years in the NBA, this version of Wemby is much harder to deal with as he's now cracking the 30 PPG mark, along with his alien shot-blocking and defensive aura. So yeah, Wemby has arrived as an offensive powerhouse now.

The San Antonio Spurs star is second in the NBA with 15.8 points per game in the paint, behind only Giannis. He's shooting 64.6% on two-point attempts and putting up 30.7 points in just 30.5 minutes per game, which works out to around 36.2 points per 36 minutes.

And unlike most centers who get that many points inside, Wemby is also attempting 6.7 threes per game. He's made 38 of those shots through 18 games, shooting 31.7% from deep. That's still below league average, but just having a center who can take that many threes changes how opposing centers guard him. And his 3.2 mid-range points per game rank 11th in the NBA, so he's getting plenty of shots between those two areas as well.

Wembanyama's shooting splits of 54.3% from the field, 31.7% from three, and 77.8% from the line give him a 63.0% true shooting percentage. If he becomes even a 36.0% three-point shooter on this kind of volume, we might be talking about the best scorer in the world within a year or two.

Jalen Brunson probably has the best post game of any point guard in the NBA not named Luka Doncic, which is funny considering he's only 6-foot-2. The New York Knicks star plays like a power forward for a few seconds every time he gets a defender on his back, using pivots, pump fakes, and little turnaround jumpers to get his points.

Brunson is fourth in the NBA in mid-range scoring at 4.8 points per game, with another 7.2 coming from inside the paint. He's not particularly explosive getting to the basket, but he's excellent at slowing down, getting defenders off balance, and using his body to create space for a shot.

Then look at what he's doing from three this season. Brunson has already made 53 triples in 18 games, shooting 39.6% on 7.4 attempts per game. He's getting more than a third of his points from beyond the arc without giving up the mid-range game that has made him so good over the past few seasons.

The problem is his current efficiency inside the arc, as he's shooting just 44.4% on two-point attempts and 42.7% from the field overall. His 54.8% true shooting percentage is easily the biggest weakness in his case for a top-three spot right now.

Still, I love how balanced Brunson's scoring game is. There aren't many guards in the NBA who are getting nearly five mid-range points, over seven paint points, and almost nine points from threes on a nightly basis.

This might be the most surprising name in the top three, but have you seen Jamal Murray's shooting numbers this season? The Canadian is averaging 25.8 points on 50.0% shooting from the field, 45.6% from three, and 88.3% from the free-throw line, almost on that elite 50/40/90 club.

That's good for a 65.5% true shooting percentage, the highest of anybody on this list. And he's doing it while taking just 16.9 shots per game, which is four fewer than Brunson and more than eight fewer than Luka.

Murray has made 52 threes through 16 games, taking 7.1 attempts per night. Those numbers alone would make him one of the best perimeter scorers in the NBA right now, but he's also in the top 10 in mid-range scoring at 3.5 points per game and is giving the Nuggets another 6.9 points inside the paint.

Obviously, playing next to Jokic helps a lot. Their two-man game gives Murray open pull-up jumpers when defenses drop, the chance to attack the rim when Jokic brings the opposing center to the break, and plenty of good looks from three. But Murray still has to make those shots, and he's doing it at an incredible rate.

He's also making 53.2% of his two-point attempts, meaning he's currently more efficient than Brunson both inside and outside the arc while averaging almost the same number of points.

I wouldn't necessarily have Murray third if we were talking about pure shot creation over the last few years. But if we're ranking these guys based on what they're doing right now, it's very difficult to argue against his combination of scoring volume, shot versatility, and efficiency.

There's really not much of a debate on Shai Gilgeous-Alexander being the best inside-the-arc scorer among guards in the NBA. The Oklahoma City Thunder's reigning MVP is getting around 18 points per game between his paint and mid-range scoring, and nobody else on this list comes close to his production from the mid-range.

SGA leads the entire league with 7.7 mid-range points per game, 1.7 more than second-place Barnes and 2.2 more than Booker. Almost a quarter of his scoring comes from mid-range jumpers alone, which is ridiculous for a guy averaging over 32 points in today's NBA.

What I love about his game is that he doesn't need a ton of space to get where he wants. He can change speeds three or four times on a single drive, get a defender leaning in one direction, and stop for a baseline jumper before the help defense gets there.

And his three-point volume has gone up quite a bit this season, too. Without Jalen Williams, Cason Wallace, or Chet Holmgren around, Shai is taking 6.6 threes per game compared to 4.4 last year, making 43 of his first 119 attempts for a 36.1% shooting percentage. He's also getting another 6.8 points per night at the free-throw line, maybe his best skill set.

His overall efficiency has actually gone down from last season, when he shot 55.3% from the field with a 66.5% true shooting percentage. He's currently at 48.0% and 58.3%, respectively, which is worth keeping in mind even with his higher scoring average, as he's obviously had to carry an even bigger burden without 3 starters.

I'd probably have Shai first if his three-point game were closer to Luka's. But considering what Doncic is doing from beyond the arc while still ranking among the best mid-range scorers in the league, I've got SGA just behind him.

How do you even guard a guy who's giving you almost 15 points from three while also being one of the best post-up guards in basketball? That's basically what teams are dealing with every time they face Luka Doncic and the Los Angeles Lakers this season.

Doncic leads the NBA in scoring at 36.6 points per game, 4.5 more than Shai, while also having a league-leading 39.0% usage rate. He's made 77 threes through 16 games, shooting 36.5% on a crazy 13.2 attempts per game, when 65.1% of those come unassisted.

That's 231 points from three-pointers alone. For comparison, Shai has made 43 threes in two more games, while Murray has made 52 in the same number of appearances. Nobody on this list is getting anywhere near Luka's scoring production from deep right now.

But here's where it gets even better. Doncic is also fifth in the NBA in mid-range scoring with 4.6 points per game, and he's currently at 81.6% in the restricted area. He's making 56.6% of his two-point attempts while also taking the most difficult shots in his arsenal on a regular basis.

He's also getting to the free-throw line 10.2 times per game, converting 86.5% of those attempts and scoring another 8.8 points per night from there. His true shooting percentage is at around 62.1%, which is quite impressive considering his 25 FGA per game and how many of them are threes.

For me, the difference between Luka and everybody else is how much pressure he puts on a defense at all three levels without needing anyone else to help him out. He's not as efficient as Murray from three or as productive as Shai from the mid-range, but combining that kind of perimeter volume with his finishing and post game is something nobody else in the NBA is doing right now.

#2622. Lakers biggest test is coming, but it’s not Spurs, per JJ Redick

The Lakers' biggest test of the season is coming up.

"Whether we lose the game, whether we win the game, we're either going to be contenders on [ESPN's] 'First Take' or we're not going to be contenders and we're fake," Lakers coach JJ Redick said. "That stuff is just noise."

For the Lakers, their upcoming game against the Spurs is a temperature check.

The teams are tied for the best record in the NBA at 15-3. And their stars, Luka Doncic and Victor Wembanyama, are in a two-man race for the MVP Award.

In other words, this is prime theater. And we all know what that means.

San Antonio Spurs center Victor Wembanyama dunks against the Portland Trail Blazers in Portland, Ore., Wednesday, Nov. 25, 2026. AP Photo/Craig Mitchelldyer

If the Lakers win, they'll be the front-runners for the title. Doncic will officially be ahead of Wembanyama in the MVP race. The darlings of the NBA will be the crown jewel of the basketball world.

But if they lose, well, the opposite will happen. There will be some version of sound the alarm. Press the panic button. The Lakers aren't elite. Doncic isn't the real deal. Walker Kessler can't compete against the league's top centers.

Luka Doncic (77) of the Los Angeles Lakers handles the ball against the Utah Jazz on Monday, Nov. 23, 2026, at Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles. NBAE via Getty Images

When they win, they're the talk of the town. When they lose, the sky is falling. They inspire overreactions. They're the dream fodder for pundits.

Los Angeles Lakers head coach JJ Redick watches his players during an NBA basketball game against the Utah Jazz in Los Angeles, Monday, Nov. 23, 2026. AP Photo/Kyusung Gong

There are nine new players on the Lakers. They haven't experienced the weight of that attention. It can be paralyzing. Even Doncic, who has been in the spotlight for most of his life, has never been the face of a franchise as big as the Lakers.

If the Lakers play great, they can't let it get to their heads. And if they fall apart, they need to dust their shoulders and move forward.

Championship teams lose games. But they don't allow themselves to be defined by them.

So, this game doesn't matter and yet it means everything.

It's the ultimate test for a young group. And it has nothing to do with the score.

Leeds United are among the clubs tracking Leicester City academy winger Bismark Owusu ahead of the January window, with growing competition emerging for one of the Foxes' most highly rated young attackers.

He "has made steady progress through the Foxes' youth ranks" and has remained a regular contributor this term, while also stepping up for Leicester's Under-21s in the Premier League Cup and Premier League 2.

There has been no senior debut yet, although the assessment from the report is clear, Owusu "is very highly rated". That matters when clubs are planning for the medium and long term, especially in a market where top-end young talent is increasingly identified earlier and pursued more aggressively.

A key factor in this developing story is contractual status. Owusu "only recently turned 18 and is not yet tied to a professional contract at Leicester", which naturally increases external interest and places pressure on Leicester to act quickly. The club will want to keep hold of a player with clear upside, but TeamTalk adds that "the volume of interest from both English and continental clubs means they face a challenge in keeping him".

That challenge is sharpened by recent history. Leicester have already seen elite academy talent move on, most notably Jeremy Monga's exit to Manchester City in a £12.5million deal last summer. In that context, Owusu's future becomes one to monitor carefully as January approaches.

For Leeds, this feels like the type of move modern recruitment departments often explore early, before a prospect's value rises further. TeamTalk says "Leeds and Brentford are both exploring the possibility of a move when the January window opens", while "sources have also added Crystal Palace to the mix". Italian and Dutch clubs are also said to be monitoring the player.

Another detail could prove relevant in any cross-border interest. The report notes that "The youngster's of an Italian passport, in addition to eligibility for England and Ghana, is seen as a potential advantage for any clubs looking to complete a deal around Europe."

At this stage, "No formal bids or advanced negotiations for Owusu have been confirmed", but the direction of travel is obvious. Leicester are "working hard to secure the future of a talent who has serious potential", while Leeds and others weigh whether admiration turns into a concrete move.

This is exactly the sort of report that grabs the attention. Leeds have shown before that they are prepared to think beyond the obvious, and Owusu sounds like a player being identified before he reaches the wider spotlight. When a young winger posts 12 goals and seven assists at Under-18 level, clubs do not watch by accident.

The intriguing part is the profile. A right-sided attacker with production, age on his side and room to develop fits the kind of signing that can strengthen the pipeline rather than demand immediate first-team pressure. That feels sensible, especially if the club are trying to build depth with genuine upside instead of chasing only expensive, ready-made options.

There is also a familiar warning in this. If Brentford and Crystal Palace are involved, Leeds will know the competition is serious and well informed. Those clubs tend to do their homework. Add interest from Italy and the Netherlands, and it becomes clear that this is no casual link.

The contract angle makes it even more interesting. If Leicester have not yet secured him professionally, there may be an opening, but these situations can change quickly. The important thing is that Leeds are present early. Supporters will always get excited by senior names, but well-timed academy recruitment can be just as important. If this one progresses, it could be a very smart piece of business.

#2619. The Jordan Clarkson moment that shows why Knicks’ unique bench works so well

It was a guy who didn't play who served as a catalyst for the Knicks' most all-around win this year.

Coach Mike Brown used 12 players in the team's 121-102 win over the Cavs on Wednesday night at Madison Square Garden. Without OG Anunoby (calf strain) and Miles McBride (adductor tightness), it meant end-of-the-bench reserves got a rare chance to see some action.

Pacôme Dadiet had seven points in 14 minutes. Rookie Tyler Nickel, making his NBA debut (he has spent this year in the G League), got nine minutes and had five points. Mohamed Diawara got four minutes and chipped in three points. James Wiseman saw six minutes of action and helped seal the win with a few crucial rebounds late — he finished with six offensive rebounds.

Under Brown's anything-goes system, nobody is too far away from getting a chance. His love of experimentation, particularly early in the year, means players seemingly out of the rotation will get their opportunity to prove themselves at some point.

Jordan Clarkson of the New York Knicks smiles before an NBA basketball game against the Indiana Pacers in Indianapolis, Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. NBAE via Getty Images

It has cultivated an ego-less culture among the bench players, where they know the minutes will look different every night. It's a system of basketball socialism of sorts. But it's only possible because one member of that group set the tone for the rest.

"As a coach, you could want to do that, but you have to have others around you that will at least support it initially to see how it turns out," Brown said. "And a huge, huge, huge catalyst for that was Jordan Clarkson. Jordan Clarkson was the one, if you're talking about giving 100 percent out there to what allows me to do that, I think Jordan Clarkson gave me at least 90 percent of the opportunity to do it, because here's an accomplished veteran that could be in the rotation for almost any team out there, let alone a championship team, and I can literally play him six straight games and then sit him 10 straight games and he's gonna be the same dude every fricken' day. And he's gonna talk the same way to his teammates. Not 'can you believe what Mike Brown did?' Nah, he's gonna be the same dude, uplift the group, and then when I call his number again, he's gonna be ready to go.

"He's a guy that, even when he gets done playing, it's one of those things where you hope that he can just be a part of this organization in some way, shape or form until he doesn't want to be part of this organization. He's that type of person, in my opinion."

Clarkson missed Wednesday's game — the fourth straight he's been sidelined due to plantar fasciitis. But it was he who helped Dadiet — who has largely underwhelmed, now in his third year after the Knicks drafted him in the first round — deliver his best game as a pro.

"JC is always big on that, telling guys to stay ready," Jose Alvarado said. "He was in [Dadiet's] ear the whole shootaround [Wednesday morning]. Just telling everybody to stay ready because you never know when your name is called."

New York Knicks forward Pacome Dadiet (4) puts up a shot against the Cleveland Cavaliers at Madison Square Garden in New York, Wednesday, Nov. 25, 2026. Jason Szenes for NY Post

Alvarado himself had his best game of the year with 21 points in 19 minutes. But it wasn't long ago that he was out of the rotation, with Tyler Kolek having usurped him as the backup point guard.

But Brown has recently been experimenting with having Alvarado on the floor at the same time as Jalen Brunson, in order to allow Brunson to play off-the-ball more. And Brown has liked the results.

That has meant Alvarado is now cutting back into Kolek's minutes, despite Kolek continuing to play well. That could rub other players on other teams the wrong way –— losing minutes despite not doing anything wrong, simply because the coach wants to try something new and see how it works out. For the bench players, nothing is set in stone, regardless of how you play.

This team embraces it, though. Brown compared the way this bench pulls for one another to the championship Spurs and Warriors teams he was an assistant on.

"We care about each other," Landry Shamet, currently the top dog of that bench unit, said. "We want to win for each other. We're willing to take on different roles and we know that we've got each other's back. If Jose's got it going and my minutes are shortened, awesome. And vice versa. All of us, Deuce [McBride] included in that, I would throw him in that as well, all of us kind of feel that way. That's really cool.

"I've been saying it, I've been a broken record about it, but you don't see that — that's very rare where no ego or ulterior motives get involved. That's something special that you want to be a part of."

Something special, sparked by a special personality in Clarkson.
